entries.section: (1) Introduction and greeting

paragraphs.text: Achaia: the southern region of Greece. The Romans made Corinth the capital of Achaia.

St. Paul the Apostle begins by mentioning his name, to confirm that he is the writer of the epistle, together with his disciple Timothy, who had visited Corinth. He declares that God chose him as His apostle, to please Him and to do His will.

entries.section: (1) Introduction and greeting

paragraphs.text: He sends them grace and peace. God is the source of grace, for He has graciously granted us salvation. This also shows the oneness of the Father with the Son as one source of grace and peace.

The Church took up this prayer and made it a blessing for the people at their dismissal, so the priest says, "The love of God the Father, the grace of His only-begotten Son, and the communion and gift and operation of the Holy Spirit be with you."

Every Christian has a mission that he received from God on the day of his baptism, which is the salvation of his soul and witness to Christ in the world, and every grace in his life has God as its source. So thank God every day for the grace He gives you, and try to invest these graces so that you may enjoy them, and your fellowship with God will increase.

entries.section: (2) God is the source of comfort

paragraphs.text: The Father of our Lord Jesus Christ: the hypostasis of the Father.
The Father of mercies: the source of all compassion, mercy and tenderness.
The God of all comfort: the wellspring of comfort and support for all people.
Paul affirms that there is no mercy, compassion or comfort apart from God, because He is the source and father of all mercy and comfort.

entries.section: (2) God is the source of comfort

paragraphs.text: Comforts us: supports us, makes us feel His presence with us, and gladdens our hearts.

God is the source of all comfort, and He is the One who comforted the Apostles and the saints in all their afflictions and trials. All the Apostles experienced this comfort, because they were exposed to many sufferings and the Lord was with them and comforted them. Comfort is not only, at times, the prevention of affliction, but God's support of us in it, so that it does not harm us. This made the suffering Apostles and saints able to comfort those in distress as well and to lighten their pains.

entries.section: (2) God is the source of comfort

paragraphs.text: The Apostle encourages the Corinthians to face the afflictions they meet, telling them that as afflictions and sufferings increase, God's grace to them will increase, so that they will experience His work in them and feel His presence with them. This is the greatest thing in existence, indeed it is a pledge of the Kingdom.

entries.section: (2) God is the source of comfort

paragraphs.text: Your salvation, which is effective: that is, the grace of Christ working in the one who believes, so that he may endure sufferings and remain firm in the faith.

St. Paul declares that he and his fellow servants endure labors and afflictions for the sake of the preaching, so that the Corinthians may obtain salvation through Christ. The believers in Corinth, at the same time, endure sufferings because of their adherence to the faith.

And if the Apostle and the servants receive comforts from God in their service, they make those they serve share in them as well, for they tell them of God's work in the ministry, so that they are comforted and rejoice with the Apostles.

entries.section: (2) God is the source of comfort

paragraphs.text: The Apostle affirms his confidence and hope concerning the believers in the Church of Corinth: if they endure sufferings, they will also receive comforts and support from God.

May we feel that every pain and affliction in our life is a sharing in the sufferings of Christ, and Christ Himself, who suffered for us, will not leave us, but will comfort us and strengthen us. As great as our suffering and weariness, so great will be our joys and God's support of us.

entries.section: (3) Paul as an example in enduring afflictions

paragraphs.text: Asia: not the continent of Asia, but the western part of Asia Minor, which is present-day Turkey.
Paul presents himself as an example by what happened to him of afflictions in Asia. These afflictions made Paul feel discouraged and despairing of escaping with his life from death.

entries.section: (3) Paul as an example in enduring afflictions

paragraphs.text: The afflictions and dangers to which Paul was exposed were expected to end in his death. Therefore, having lost every human strength and thought of deliverance, he had no recourse but to trust in God, who is able to raise him from the dead even if he died.

entries.section: (3) Paul as an example in enduring afflictions

paragraphs.text: God delivered Paul from the sentence of death, and He will deliver him again from all dangers, because God does not change; He is the same yesterday, today and forever (Heb 13:8). God delivers His children at all times, and then the affliction becomes a spiritual experience that supports a person when he is exposed to afflictions in the future.

entries.section: (3) Paul as an example in enduring afflictions

paragraphs.text: By many persons... through many: the believers in Corinth and the other churches who pray for Paul and his companions.

The Corinthians gave Paul help, which was prayer on his behalf, that the Lord might deliver him from all afflictions. Therefore God granted him deliverance and strength to endure sufferings, and this led them to give thanks to God.

If you live as a stranger to the world and are occupied with preparing for eternal life, your being affected will be limited and bearable when afflictions meet you. So control your desires and do not cling to material things, so that you may grow in your relationship with God and thus endure the afflictions of life.

entries.section: (4) Paul's ministry and preaching

paragraphs.text: St. Paul declares that his actions are in simplicity, relying on the grace of God and not on human wisdom. He had wanted to go to them from Ephesus, but for many reasons he changed his mind, and some doubted him, thinking he was not wise. So he explained to them that he does not act by his own thoughts, but in simplicity submits to the Holy Spirit, and God guides him.

entries.section: (4) Paul's ministry and preaching

paragraphs.text: Other things: we do not mean anything else, hidden and different from what is plain in our words.
What you read or acknowledge: what you understood from our words, because our words are frank and clear.
You shall acknowledge to the end: Paul makes clear that whoever does not know him well and doubts him will know him afterward and trust him.
In part: some believers did not know Paul fully and trust him completely, so their knowledge of him was partial and would be completed with the passing of time.

The Apostle shows that his words are frank and he means nothing but what he wrote. Some thought he wrote words by which he meant something else. But he affirms that his words are simple, frank and clear.

Some of the believers in Corinth had known Paul and trusted him, while others did not yet trust him. So he tells them that in the end they will know him as their apostle who is clear in his words to them. And when Christ comes in His Second Coming, the believers in Corinth will boast in being Paul's children, just as he will boast in being their father.

entries.section: (4) Paul's ministry and preaching

paragraphs.text: Paul's confidence in his fatherhood to them, and their holding fast to their sonship to him, made him plan to come from Ephesus to Corinth, then go to Macedonia and return to them to visit them a second time and confirm their faith, on his way back from Macedonia to Jerusalem and Judea.

entries.section: (4) Paul's ministry and preaching

paragraphs.text: I was minded to come: that is, to visit Corinth before reaching Macedonia.
Lightness: haste and impulsiveness in thinking.
According to the flesh: human purposes, and not the guidance of the Holy Spirit.
Yea yea... nay nay: I declare truths and then draw back from them and say the opposite.

St. Paul asks in protest about what had happened: he first thought of going from Ephesus to Corinth and then Macedonia, then changed his mind and went directly to Macedonia. He asks whether his first plan was made with human haste or had a personal purpose. The answer, of course, is no, because he moves by the guidance of the Holy Spirit. His thought was to visit Corinth, but God guided him to go to Macedonia first and then return to Corinth. His enemies thought that he was speaking contradictory words, announcing that he would visit Corinth and then retracting his word and not visiting it, so that they concluded from this that all his preaching was doubtful, and what he said about Christ could be retracted and changed.

entries.section: (4) Paul's ministry and preaching

paragraphs.text: God is true: God is witness to what I say, as a confirmation and assurance of the truth of his words. Our word toward you: the preaching of Christ.
Paul affirms that his word is true, and God is witness to this, that his preaching to them was truthful, and that he did not say anything he could retract or change.

entries.section: (4) Paul's ministry and preaching

paragraphs.text: Silvanus: he is Silas.
Was not yea and nay: it is not possible to change or retract any truth they heard about Christ in the preaching to them.
In Him is yea: that is, a firm truth that does not change, namely the truths of the preaching of Christ.

The Apostle affirms that the eternal Christ, in whom there is no change at all, whom Paul and his companions preached in Corinth, is true and firm, and it is not possible to change any truth they heard about Him.

entries.section: (4) Paul's ministry and preaching

paragraphs.text: The yea... and the Amen: the fulfillment of all the divine promises, because they are true.
By us: these divine promises were preached by Paul and his companions.

However great God's promises are, such as the acceptance of sinners and their justification and the support of His children in the hardest afflictions, all of this is true and will be accomplished so that God may be glorified in those who believe in Him.

entries.section: (5) Paul's longsuffering

paragraphs.text: Anointed us: the anointing with the Myron that takes place after Baptism.
God: that is, the Holy Spirit.
Sealed us: the sign of the cross made with the oil on all the members of the person is a divine seal declaring that these members have become God's possession, working for Him.

The source of our spiritual steadfastness is God, through our anointing with the Holy Spirit in the Sacrament of Myron, which is therefore called the Sacrament of Confirmation, and the Holy Spirit gives us the knowledge of God as a pledge of the perfect knowledge in eternity.

entries.section: (5) Paul's longsuffering

paragraphs.text: I call God for a record upon my soul: confirmation of the truth of what I say.
Not that we have dominion over your faith: that is, we do not want to control you.

Helpers of your joy: supporting you and confirming your faith so that you may rejoice with true joy. By faith ye stand: true faith is what establishes a person in Christ so that he rejoices. Paul explains truthfully before God a fact, which is that he did not come to Corinth in order to spare the believers there, because he would be compelled to rebuke them for their sins. This is not domination over them, but he wishes to support them on the way of their salvation and to rejoice in their joy with Christ.
Do you accept the guidance and rebukes of the Fathers and spiritual guides so that you repent and correct your mistakes?
And know that this is the way of your steadfastness in the spiritual life, and when you accept guidance you live a life of repentance, stand firm in the faith, and rejoice with true joy.
The Church's discipline of the sinner and thanking God for His work

entries.section: (1) The reasons for Paul's not coming to Corinth

paragraphs.text: I determined: I resolved.
In heaviness: I grieve over your clinging to sin and rebuke you for your sins, and you grieve.

Who is he then that maketh me glad: Paul rejoices in their repentance and grieves over their lack of repentance, so he wishes to come to them after they repent through this epistle, and so rejoice in them.
This same: that is, what is written in the two preceding verses.

Paul decided not to visit Corinth because of their falling into many sins, and he would be compelled to rebuke them and they would grieve, and he did not want to grieve them. So he postponed the visit and sent this epistle, in which he calls them to repentance, so that when he visits them he may rejoice in their repentance, because the source of his joy is the repentance and joy of his children. How then could he grieve them with severe rebuke?!
Paul trusts in their love of God, so when they find him joyful at his visit to them, they will rejoice too, because love is strong between them and him.
The Second Epistle of Paul the Apostle to the Corinthians

entries.section: (1) The reasons for Paul's not coming to Corinth

paragraphs.text: When Paul learned of their sins, he grieved over them and wrote them this epistle with tears flowing for them, seeking their repentance. By this the Corinthians come to know the extent of his fatherhood and his love for sinners, especially the Corinthians. So they should not be upset by his rebuke, but feel his love and hasten to repentance.

My brother, when you speak to others, may you feel their feelings and not condemn them, but let your true aim in every word to them be love. True love makes us warn, guide, and sometimes rebuke those we love, but with love, gentleness and a spirit of meekness.

entries.section: (2) The Church's discipline

paragraphs.text: If any... such a one: he means the sinner in Corinth who was mentioned in the first epistle, who committed fornication with his father's wife, and Paul excommunicated him from the Church for a period so that he might repent (1 Cor 5:1). This sinner grieved not only the Apostle Paul, but the whole Church, because all are one body. So that Paul might not make the punishment on him heavier than this, he asked the Church, that is, the priests, to lift the excommunication from him and to restore him to partaking of the Holy Mysteries after he had spent the period of punishment and repentance.

entries.section: (2) The Church's discipline

paragraphs.text: Overmuch sorrow: despair.
Confirm your love toward him: show your love and your concern for him.
Paul asked them to forgive him, encourage him and show their love for him, so that despair would not overcome him.

entries.section: (2) The Church's discipline

paragraphs.text: The proof of you: your virtues and distinction as children of Paul, which appear in their obedience to him. Paul makes clear that their response to this word of his will show the extent of their obedience, and he affirms that they are his true children. That is, he asks for their obedience to him in forgiving this offender.

entries.section: (2) The Church's discipline

paragraphs.text: In the person of Christ: Paul feels that he is gathered with the believers in Corinth in the Church, and Christ is in their midst, so they are able to decide on the return of this sinner.
Lest Satan should get an advantage of us: lest he seize an opportunity and take any soul on the way of evil.
His devices: his attempts to make human beings fall.

Paul also declares that he forgave this sinner for the sake of his love for them, and consequently he loves this sinner, since he is one of his children. For he does not want any of them to remain in sin, whether by persisting in it if he is not punished, or, if the punishment is increased, by falling into despair of the possibility of repentance. By this we prevent the devil, who wants to make us fall into sin in any form, from prevailing.

We always pray in our prayers that God forgive us our trespasses, as we also forgive those who trespass against us. May we make peace with people and forgive them as God forgives us and pardons our mistakes. May we also forget people's weaknesses and not recall them to them, because the Lord says to us, "I will remember their sin no more" (Jer 31:34).

entries.section: (3) Why did Paul not stay in Troas?

paragraphs.text: Paul went from Ephesus to Troas to preach Christ. There a new door for preaching was opened to him, to cross over to the region of Macedonia, which is northern Greece.
The Second Epistle of Paul the Apostle to the Corinthians

entries.section: (3) Why did Paul not stay in Troas?

paragraphs.text: My brother: it is humility on Paul's part to call his son Titus "his brother."

Here Paul's feelings and humility appear, as he felt the lack of his son Titus, who was not with him, but this did not hinder him from continuing to preach, so he went from Troas to preach in the region of Macedonia.

It is good to be bound by feelings of love to those around you, so that you rejoice in their presence and miss them if they leave you. But do not be hindered from completing your worship or your service or your work if one of your loved ones leaves you, but lean on God, the source of love and help, and continue your life with zeal and strength.

entries.section: (4) Thanksgiving to God for the success of the Gospel

paragraphs.text: Triumph: Paul feels that he walks with the servants and the believers in the Church as a company triumphing, with Christ as their leader, over the devil.

Paul thanks God, who made him a servant and a preacher in His name, so that he triumphs over the devil and gathers the souls that were under his grip and draws them to faith. By this Christ appears in Paul's life and in his preaching like a sweet fragrance that spreads quickly among those to whom he preaches in every place where he preached.

entries.section: (4) Thanksgiving to God for the success of the Gospel

paragraphs.text: St. Paul declares that his preaching makes the hearers know Christ the Savior and spreads among them like a sweet fragrance, whether those who receive the word of life and so obtain salvation and new life, or those who reject it, so that the words of preaching condemn them and become a judgment against them on the Day of Judgment and lead them to eternal death.

Then he asks concerning the greatness of the ministry of preaching, saying, who is able to perform this ministry? The answer: no one, except by the grace of God that works in him and in all the servants to make souls know Christ and draw them to faith.

entries.section: (4) Thanksgiving to God for the success of the Gospel

paragraphs.text: Paul describes the qualities of the true servant, giving himself as an example. These qualities are:
1- Frankness and the absence of deceit or trickery in proclaiming Christ the Savior; he neither adds nor changes anything, as the heretics do.
2- He preaches sincerely with all his strength to win souls.
3- He prays and asks for God's help, because the power of preaching is by God's grace and power ("of God in Christ").
4- He feels that he is in the presence of God as he speaks, so he is at ease, and also in reverence, during his ministry ("before God").

May we thank God before every work and after it, because everything is accomplished by His power. In this way we are saved from pride or faint-heartedness, and are not troubled by the scarcity or abundance of fruit, but remain steadfast in our service and our works and feel the presence of God more in our life.
A comparison between the Law and the New Testament

entries.section: (1) Paul is worthy to preach

paragraphs.text: Paul affirms that he does not need to commend himself to his disciples by what he offers them, nor does he need letters of recommendation to them or from them, as some preachers did, because he is known among them as an apostle, and his works among them bear witness to him.

entries.section: (1) Paul is worthy to preach

paragraphs.text: Having declared that he has no need of letters of recommendation to the Corinthians, Paul offers the alternative, namely the believers in Corinth, and counts them as his epistle, which is not written on paper but in his heart, that is, he loves them and prays for them. On the other hand, this epistle, that is, the believers in Corinth, is visible before the believers of the other churches as proof of Paul's preaching. They are a living epistle that every person sees when he learns of the faith and strength of the Church of Corinth, especially since it is a city famous in the world.

entries.section: (1) Paul is worthy to preach

paragraphs.text: Paul affirms that the believers in Corinth are an epistle from God to the whole world, and it was written through Paul's ministry and preaching among them.

This epistle differs from letters of recommendation in that the first is written by the work of the Holy Spirit in the believers, while the second is merely ink on paper. This epistle also differs from, and is more exalted than, God's message to His people in the Old Testament, which was the Ten Commandments written on two tables of stone, whereas Christ's epistle in the Church of Corinth is the fleshy hearts of the believers who live with God.

entries.section: (1) Paul is worthy to preach

paragraphs.text: Paul does not need letters of recommendation for the Corinthians to trust him, but the faith of these believers in Corinth gives him confidence, through the power of Christ before God, that he is an apostle and a faithful servant.

entries.section: (1) Paul is worthy to preach

paragraphs.text: After declaring that his preaching in Corinth is the proof of his apostleship, and is the letter of recommendation that confirms the success of his ministry and his sincerity, he declares that this ministry is by the power of God and not his own power; he is not sufficient in himself, but by the work of God.

Do you feel that you are responsible for ministering to those around you and for presenting Christ to them alive in your life and conduct? Do you care for them spiritually and bind them to the Church? Do you give them love and care for their needs?
This is your mission in life: to offer love and to care for everyone, especially those around you.

entries.section: (2) The glory of the New Testament

paragraphs.text: It is Christ who made Paul and his companions sufficient for this ministry and able to perform it. The ministry of the New Testament is distinguished from the ministry of the Old Testament in that it shows the spiritual depths of the commandment and its effect on the person, whereas the Jews understood the commandments of the Old Testament literally and did not know their depths. Likewise, the commandments of the Old Testament exposed the sins of human beings and condemned them to its penalty, that is, death, whereas the ministry of the New Testament is what helped believers to carry out the commandments by the power of the Holy Spirit and gave them new life in Christ.

entries.section: (2) The glory of the New Testament

paragraphs.text: Engraven in stones: the Ten Commandments written on two tables of stone; here the whole Law is meant.

The Apostle Paul makes clear that the commandments of the Law, which condemned man to death because of his inability to fulfill them, were given by God in glory, in the form of the lightnings and thunders that occurred when Moses received them on the mountain (Ex 19:16). The people were greatly afraid of this great divine glory, and even more than this, after Moses met with God his face shone, and the children of Israel could not bear to see its radiance throughout his life, so he put a veil on his face when he spoke with them, and then took it off when he went in to stand before God in the tabernacle of the congregation (Ex 34:35).

entries.section: (2) The glory of the New Testament

paragraphs.text: The Apostle continues his comparison of the ministry of the New Testament with the old, declaring that if the latter was in glory, how much more glorious will the ministry of the New Testament be, in which the Holy Spirit works.

entries.section: (2) The glory of the New Testament

paragraphs.text: The Apostle affirms the greatness of the glory of the ministry of the New Testament over the old, in that he calls the latter the ministry of condemnation, because the commandments of the Old Testament condemn man and sentence him to death, whereas the ministry of the New Testament, in which the Holy Spirit works, forgives the believer's sins and justifies him, and therefore grants him greater glory.

entries.section: (2) The glory of the New Testament

paragraphs.text: That which was made glorious: that is, Christ. In this respect: it was not given glory like Moses. The glory that excelleth: the unlimited divine glory. The Apostle adds that Moses, the leader of the ministry of the Old Testament, whom God glorified before the eyes of the people, cannot be compared in glory with Christ, who has the glory that excels over all human beings, as was shown at the Transfiguration of Christ on the mountain, with a great radiance far greater than the splendor of Moses and Elijah. For Christ is God, of perfect and unlimited glory.

entries.section: (2) The glory of the New Testament

paragraphs.text: Moses is a transient man, and the ministry of the Law is limited, lasting 1,500 years, whereas the ministry of Christ, that is, the New Testament, is permanent forever, and therefore its glory is greater. The Church in the New Testament expresses the glory of this ministry by lighting lamps during the prayers even in the daytime, as well as lighting candles and lanterns, the priest's lifting the Gospel over his head, and the people's standing in reverence at the reading of the Gospel.

It is a great grace to live in the New Testament. May you enjoy partaking of the Holy Mysteries and meditating on the words of the Holy Bible, and so experience deep prayers with God that draw your heart to the glories of eternity.

entries.section: (3) The revelation of God in the New Testament

paragraphs.text: Paul declares that he has hope and confidence in the ministry of the Gospel of the New Testament, because it is powerful and spiritual and has an excelling glory, for it depends on Christ. Therefore he speaks boldly in his preaching without fear.

entries.section: (3) The revelation of God in the New Testament

paragraphs.text: Veil: a covering or a piece of cloth.
That which is abolished: the face of Moses, which would turn to dust in the grave and its glory pass away.
The old testament: the books of the Old Testament
Is done away in Christ: upon believing in Christ.
Moses is read: the five books of Moses.
It shall turn to the Lord: by repentance and faith in Christ.

Paul makes clear that the veil which Moses used to put on his face to hide its radiance when he spoke with the children of Israel signifies the hardness of the hearts of the Jews, which is like a veil on their hearts, so that it hides from them the words of the books of the Old Testament, which they hear in their synagogues and which prophesy about Christ. But when they believe in Christ and turn back from the hardness of their hearts, they will understand the prophecies.

entries.section: (3) The revelation of God in the New Testament

paragraphs.text: The Lord: Christ.
The Spirit: the Holy Spirit.

The Apostle shows the work of the hypostases together in the New Testament. The one who believes in Christ has the Holy Spirit working in him, who is the Spirit of Christ, and when the Holy Spirit works in the believer He frees him from the condemnation of the Law upon him and gives him power and freedom to go forth in the love of God, so that he understands the commandments spiritually and not literally, and goes deeply into them and lives by them.

entries.section: (3) The revelation of God in the New Testament

paragraphs.text: The face of the Lord: Christ.
A glass: the Holy Bible, the Sacraments, and the means of grace such as prayers, fasts, and so on.
We are changed: from human life to the spirituality of the children of God.
The image: man is the image of God and the image of Christ.
From glory to glory: spiritual growth in degrees toward perfection.
The Lord the Spirit: the Holy Spirit.

When we believe in Christ, we are gradually changed from our human ways to the exaltedness of the life of the children of God, because we see Christ through the Holy Bible, we are united with Him in the Holy Sacraments, and we come to know Him through prayers, fasts and service. Thus in the New Testament God reveals Himself to us the nearer we draw to Him through spiritual striving, and by this we advance in spiritual degrees toward holiness by the power of the work of the Holy Spirit in us.

This spiritual growth will continue in eternity, so that God is revealed to us and we see Him face to face in a great revelation and not as in a glass (a limitation), and we keep discovering His love and His depths and delighting in them forever.
Today you have come into the glory of the New Testament, and you have come to see Christ and touch Him.
Has this relationship helped you to change, so that everyone who deals with you sees this glory that you have received from God, and notices this change in you?

God took a bodily form different from His nature in order to change us and make us in the image of His glory and splendor. So we must walk in purity and righteousness, and people will see our good works and glorify our Father who is in heaven.
God's blessings to His suffering servants

entries.section: (1) Paul's faithfulness in his preaching

paragraphs.text: Therefore: because of the excelling glory of the ministry of the New Testament over the ministry of the Old Testament, that is, the Law.
This ministry: the ministry of preaching the Gospel.
As we have received mercy: God turned Paul from serving the Law and persecuting the Christians to preaching the Gospel, and this is a great divine mercy.

We faint not: we do not stumble and become negligent in preaching, and so become unfaithful or failing servants. The Apostle Paul feels the greatness of the ministry of the New Testament, indeed he sees it as a great grace and mercy from God that He allows him to be His servant. Therefore he holds fast to it and performs it faithfully and does not become idle or fall short in it.

entries.section: (1) Paul's faithfulness in his preaching

paragraphs.text: The hidden things of dishonesty: shameful sins that a person is ashamed to have appear before others.
Craftiness: twisting words to achieve personal ends, as the scribes and Pharisees did with Christ.
Handling the word of God deceitfully: interpreting it according to personal purposes, or showing what pleases people and hiding what troubles them in order to win their love.
Commending ourselves: sound conduct that God approves through the pure conscience of people. In the sight of God: Paul always feels the presence of God, so he walks uprightly because God sees him.

After Paul felt the greatness of the ministry of preaching the Gospel, he took care for the purity of his heart and the uprightness of his conduct in his preaching, so as to proclaim the divine truth as God wishes and not according to his personal purposes. By this he is accepted by God, and even commended by the pure consciences of people. Thus he wins God's mercy and the hearts of his hearers.

entries.section: (1) Paul's faithfulness in his preaching

paragraphs.text: Hid: its glory, power and effect not clear.

Them that are lost: those who walk in sins, so they refuse to believe in the Gospel and eternal destruction awaits them. The Apostle declares that the preaching of the Gospel does not reach all people, although it is powerful and effective in any ordinary person, but it becomes obscure and rejected by those who walk in evil, who reject the word of God because it opposes their personal purposes.

entries.section: (1) Paul's faithfulness in his preaching

paragraphs.text: The god of this world: Satan.
The light of the glorious Gospel of Christ: the Gospel teaches us the truth and lifts us out of shameful sins so that we become children of God and know God and love Him.
The image of God: by the Incarnation of Christ He showed us the perfect image of God, so that human beings might follow His example and restore the image of God that was disfigured in them.

The reason the Gospel is hidden and obscure to those who are lost is that Satan has occupied them with sin, so they have become blind and do not see the greatness of the Gospel, and even refuse to be enlightened by its knowledge because it exposes their sins. This Gospel is the Word of God, the incarnate Christ, by whom God reveals Himself to us in a life lived among us, so that we may learn from Him and walk in the truth.

entries.section: (1) Paul's faithfulness in his preaching

paragraphs.text: The aim of Paul's preaching is to persuade people that Christ is God, their Savior and Redeemer, and he has no personal purposes, for he does not glorify himself. And if the only aim of the preaching is the glorification of Christ, Paul counts himself a bondservant consecrated to serving the Corinthians so that they may believe in Christ.

entries.section: (1) Paul's faithfulness in his preaching

paragraphs.text: St. Paul affirms that the preaching of the Gospel depends on the power of God. Just as God created light on the first day when the whole world was darkness, He also enlightens our hearts in the New Testament, and shines upon us, not with a material sun but with His Holy Spirit, that we may know God and recover our sonship to Him and be glorified in Him by this knowledge. This is through the visible image of God, that is, the incarnate Christ, in whom we have seen and from whom we learn the ability to fulfill the commandment, and we touch Him closely through the Holy Bible and the Sacraments of the Church, and are even united with Him, so that we experience His great glory in us.

God enlightens our life in the Church by His Holy Sacraments and His spiritual word. May we go deeper every day and increase in prayers and readings so that we may enjoy knowing Him, and it may appear in our conduct, and we may call many to know Him and be joined to Him.

entries.section: (2) Paul's weakness shows God's power

paragraphs.text: The treasure: the knowledge of Christ and preaching Him.
Earthen vessels: he likens himself and all the servants to weak vessels like pottery, but the greatness is in what fills them, that is, what they preach, which is the Gospel.

The Apostle shows that the power working in the ministry is the power of God, which is not hindered by the weakness of the servants, and this calls us to thank God, the source of power in the preaching, and not the gifts or abilities of the servants.

entries.section: (2) Paul's weakness shows God's power

paragraphs.text: Paul shows his weaknesses and those of the other servants during the preaching. Problems and obstacles meet them that cause them some depression because of their weakness as human beings, but the power of God does not leave them, so they do not give up but continue their ministry with zeal and persistence, enduring troubles and sufferings with thanksgiving.

For the devil, in his wars with the servants, makes them perplexed about the means by which they serve, because he opposes them and sometimes succeeds in hindering their means, but they do not despair; rather they rise again and continue the service by new means and with other people, by the power of God.

entries.section: (2) Paul's weakness shows God's power

paragraphs.text: The devil stirs up various persecutions against the servants, and they endure them because God does not leave them but supports and encourages them, so they count the sufferings of the ministry a sharing in the cross of Christ and a crown of glory for Him. The devil prevails against them and makes them fall into sin, or shows their physical weakness before the wicked, but God strengthens them and heals them and raises them up again with power, so that they continue their striving and their ministry.

entries.section: (2) Paul's weakness shows God's power

paragraphs.text: The dying of the Lord Jesus: the sufferings that the servants endure, which almost cost them their lives.
Always delivered unto death: we are continually exposed to death through persecutions.
Our mortal flesh: the weak body, liable and exposed to death.

In sum, the Apostles and servants of Christ are always ready to endure sufferings for Christ, and even control the desires of the body and its comfort and strive in worship and service, enduring every labor. Then the grace of God and His power are manifested, as He supports these weak bodies and works through them. And in proportion to the servant's surrender of his life to God and his acceptance of sufferings, he experiences the grace of God in him and feels His fellowship, and even receives the pledge of the Kingdom while on earth in inexpressible spiritual feelings. That is, God turns affliction into a blessing, and persecutions and labors become an opportunity to see God and to be with Him.

entries.section: (2) Paul's weakness shows God's power

paragraphs.text: What appears in the Apostles and servants is the endurance of sufferings and persecutions and constant exposure to death, and these sufferings are even counted as a partial death. When the believers see the steadfastness of the servants and the power of God's word in them, they hold fast to God in spiritual striving and experience new depths in life with Him.

entries.section: (2) Paul's weakness shows God's power

paragraphs.text: The sufferings that St. Paul met in his ministry did not hinder him from continuing to preach, because he believes in Christ, who strengthens him, just as David believed in ancient times and endured sufferings and persecutions and proclaimed the truth (Ps 116:10). Since Paul enjoys the same faith, he continues his preaching despite the persecutions.

"I believed, therefore have I spoken." Beloved brother, this blessed verse places all of us before a great responsibility. Faith by its nature is not mute, and Christianity spread by the preaching of the Apostles and of everyone who believed as well. So we must make our conversations and words express our faith, and if society prevents us from speaking our faith, then let our deeds speak and bear witness to our God.

entries.section: (2) Paul's weakness shows God's power

paragraphs.text: Shall present us with you: we shall all meet in the Kingdom around Christ.

Paul takes courage in enduring sufferings by looking to the glories of eternity, and he declares his faith in the final resurrection. Just as God raised up the Lord Jesus from the dead, that is, raised Christ Himself, He will also raise us up on the last day and set us with Him in the Kingdom, to be glorified with Him in return for all our labors on earth. This in turn urges us to continue striving and serving.

entries.section: (2) Paul's weakness shows God's power

paragraphs.text: All things: the Apostles' endurance of sufferings and the work of God's grace in them.

St. Paul sees that all the persecutions and sufferings that happen to him are permitted by God not only for his benefit, but also for all those to whom he preaches in Corinth, so that their faith may be confirmed and they may offer prayers for him. Thus God's grace abounds toward him through the prayers of many of the believers of Corinth, which moves him and the whole Church of Corinth to give thanks to God, and God is glorified in them.

Do you feel that every pain and trial you endure with thanksgiving and without complaint gives glory to God? Then accept it and ask for God's help, confident that this turns into a spiritual blessing in your life and glories in heaven.

entries.section: (3) Hope in eternity

paragraphs.text: Our outward man: the body.
The inward: the spirit.

He welcomes sufferings for their benefits. Even if the body is exposed to many sufferings from persecutions and the abuse of others, this does not make us feel failure in our service, because it benefits us spiritually: the spirit is bound to God through every affliction, and the person's feelings are renewed in a deeper relationship that makes him grow spiritually throughout the days of his life, through prayers and the experience of relying on God and His work within us, so we feel a spiritual fellowship and enjoy God.

entries.section: (3) Hope in eternity

paragraphs.text: Paul sees that the afflictions to which he is exposed are light and small compared with the glory he will receive in the Kingdom, which will be great, or "weighty," as he expresses it against the lightness of the affliction. On the other hand, the affliction is temporary and takes a limited time in this life, whereas the glories of the Kingdom continue forever. Indeed he encourages us that the more afflictions we endure, the more glories we receive in heaven, and these afflictions are small and limited while the glories are great and eternal.

entries.section: (3) Hope in eternity

paragraphs.text: The things which are seen: all the material things in the world.
The things which are not seen: spiritual matters and our relationship with God.

From what has gone before, the Apostle concludes how we should walk in life: we should not be concerned about earthly things if we lose them and are exposed to bodily sufferings, because all this is temporary, but let us care for our spiritual life, for it extends forever.

Do not be troubled if you lose some material things or are exposed to abuse from those around you. All these things are transient, but try to take refuge in God and seize opportunities to be with Him, so that you enjoy His fellowship and prepare your heart for the eternal Kingdom.
Preparing for eternity and calling people to reconciliation with God

entries.section: (1) Life in eternity and preparing for it

paragraphs.text: Dissolved: torn down.

Paul says that every believer knows with certainty and faith that if he dies or is martyred as a result of the afflictions, sufferings or hardships around him, he has in heaven an eternal, abiding life. He likens the body to an earthly tent that can be taken down at any time, but when it is taken down it transfers us to a great heavenly building not made with hands, and God will clothe us with a body of light, by which is meant the body of the resurrection.

entries.section: (1) Life in eternity and preparing for it

paragraphs.text: This: the tent, that is, the body.
We groan: we ache from the sufferings and persecutions that pass over us in life.
Clothed upon: our fleshly bodies are changed into bodies of light.
Our house which is from heaven: our bodies of light, with which we will live in the Kingdom.

When Paul suffers during his life on earth, his heart is lifted to heaven, and he longs for the body of light that he will receive, which is not exposed to pain and lasts forever. Perhaps Paul, in the intensity of his longing for heaven, wished that Christ would come in His Second Coming during Paul's life on earth, and then he would not die and have his body placed in the tomb, but the material body would be changed and he would be clothed upon with a body of light, that is, the material body would be changed and disappear and become a body of light suited to being in heaven, as he mentioned this matter in (1 Cor 15:51, 52).

entries.section: (1) Life in eternity and preparing for it

paragraphs.text: Clothed: spiritual bodies.
Naked: the spirit without a body.

The Apostle continues his talk about his longing for the Second Coming and the change of the earthly body into a body of light, saying that he will be clothed with this new body and his spirit will not be found naked without a body. That is, man will live in heaven with his spirit and his body, but with a new body of light that befits life in heaven.

entries.section: (1) Life in eternity and preparing for it

paragraphs.text: St. Paul affirms that the labors of the body make him long, not for death and for placing his body in the tomb, but for the swift coming of Christ, so that his body is changed into a body of light. He likens the body of light to a garment that covers the earthly body and swallows it up. Thus the earthly is changed into the luminous.

entries.section: (1) Life in eternity and preparing for it

paragraphs.text: Hath wrought us: created us.
For the selfsame thing: to live in the Kingdom.
The earnest of the Spirit: a taste of a spiritual relationship with God on earth.

Paul shows that God's purpose in creating us is that we live with Him in heaven, and that our earthly life is temporary. Therefore He gives us, by the Holy Spirit, the pledge of the Kingdom of Heaven while we are on earth; that is, He gives us the enjoyment of a relationship with God through spiritual practices and the Sacraments of the Church, so that we may be able to bear the labors of earth and at the same time our longings toward heaven increase.

entries.section: (1) Life in eternity and preparing for it

paragraphs.text: At home in the body: attached to the desires of the body.
The Apostle affirms a firm truth, which is that if we are occupied with bodily desires, we shall become strangers to God, far from the spiritual life.

entries.section: (1) Life in eternity and preparing for it

paragraphs.text: The believing children of God see God by faith, so they are not occupied with the evil desires of the body that they see with their eyes, because they fear God and love Him and prepare for eternity.

entries.section: (1) Life in eternity and preparing for it

paragraphs.text: The natural condition of the children of God is to keep away from evil desires so as to become true children of God, that is, citizens fit for the life of heaven.

entries.section: (1) Life in eternity and preparing for it

paragraphs.text: The purpose and goal of man's life is to please God, whether he is in the body on earth or has left the body and been lifted up to heaven. Those on earth and those in heaven have the same goal, which is to please God.

entries.section: (1) Life in eternity and preparing for it

paragraphs.text: We must appear before the judgment seat of Christ: the Last Judgment.
The things done in his body: man's works on earth.

In sum, we must not forget that we shall stand before God on the Day of Judgment and be held to account for all our words, works and thoughts, and we shall be rewarded with the Kingdom if we have done good, or punished with eternal torment if we have done evil.

Do you think of heaven and feel that your earthly life is only a brief period and that we must go from the land of exile to Paradise? Do you long for God and feel the weight of the material things that deprive you of God and of fellowship with Him?

Therefore strive with all your strength to have on this earth fellowship with God and pleasing works and a constant love for His Kingdom, so that you may enjoy constant fellowship with Him in heaven, and reach that place from which sorrow, gloom and sighing have fled away.

entries.section: (2) Paul's defense of himself before the false teachers

paragraphs.text: The terror of the Lord: that is, remembering always the Day of Judgment, so that we leave sin and live for righteousness.
We persuade men: preaching Christ the Savior and preparing for eternity.

As Paul remembers the Last Judgment, the fear of God arises in him, and he preaches and teaches accordingly so that all may prepare for eternity. And as he fears God, he feels that God sees all that is within him, of estrangement from evil desires and longing for the spiritual life. He wishes that the believers in Corinth would know and understand this by their living conscience, that is, the voice of God in them, meaning that they would trust Paul that he fears God and cares for his eternity.

entries.section: (2) Paul's defense of himself before the false teachers

paragraphs.text: In appearance: outward boasting, not real.

St. Paul did not intend, in defending himself, to praise himself, but wanted to establish his apostleship in order to confirm his teachings, and when the believers in Corinth see his strong relationship with God, they answer the false teachers, who cast doubt on his teachings and boast of outward matters in order to turn the believers away from the sound faith that Paul proclaims.

entries.section: (2) Paul's defense of himself before the false teachers

paragraphs.text: The false teachers accused Paul of mental derangement, and perhaps the greatest reason was his concern for preaching to the Gentiles, at which the Jews were enraged and accused him of derangement. He accepts being accused of derangement for the sake of serving God, but he warns the believers in Corinth that he is sane in every teaching with which he preached to them, and that there is no delirium or derangement in his teachings to them about Christ.

Defend yourself for the sake of God's glory and His service, not to glorify yourself and your honor. Seek the glory of God and not your own glory, and endure sufferings for His sake, and He will glorify you in the eyes of people, even if after a while, and then in the Kingdom of Heaven.

entries.section: (3) Reconciling people with God so that they live for His love

paragraphs.text: The love of Christ constraineth us: it overwhelms us and urges us to love Him.
One: Christ.
For: instead of.

Christ died for us, so that instead of all of us dying, He died in our place. By His death our death was accomplished, and by His resurrection we all rise. How great is His love for us, for He bought us with His blood so that we may live for Him all our days.

entries.section: (3) Reconciling people with God so that they live for His love

paragraphs.text: St. Paul affirms here that Christ's death for us not only moves us to die to sin by leaving it, but we feel that we belong to Him, because He bought us with His blood, so we rise with Him to live for Him and to live in righteousness.

entries.section: (3) Reconciling people with God so that they live for His love

paragraphs.text: We know no man after the flesh: that is, as being a Jew or a Gentile, poor or rich, a man or a woman.....
Christ after the flesh: Christ as a man living as a Jewish man.
Yet now henceforth know we him no more: after faith we see Christ the God and Savior.

Since Christ bought us who believe in Him and we have become righteous in Him, we do not look at other believers according to their human circumstances, their race, and their social and financial standing, but we look at them as children of God and members of the Church. And also Christ, we see Him as God the Savior, the head of the Church, and not merely a good Jewish man who lived for a period of time on earth.

entries.section: (3) Reconciling people with God so that they live for His love

paragraphs.text: If we believe in Christ we receive the Sacrament of Baptism, in which we are born anew, and obtain a new nature, that is, we become a new creation that inclines to righteousness and keeps away from sin. Thus old things pass away from us, that is, sins and the passing concerns of the world, and we incline to imitate God and please Him, and all our senses and abilities become pure, seeking life with God.

entries.section: (3) Reconciling people with God so that they live for His love

paragraphs.text: All things: the believers in Christ who have received the new nature.
The ministry of reconciliation or the word of reconciliation: preaching reconciliation between God and man, that is, preaching Christianity.

The renewal of all believers is a grace from God, who removed the enmity and the barrier between us and Him, which is sin, by the death of Christ for us. By this we were reconciled with God, because the cause of the quarrel and separation, which is sin, has been removed, and this is what we receive in the Sacraments of Baptism, confession and Communion. His love for mankind increased in that He gave some of His children to proclaim and preach to others reconciliation with God, and this is the ministry carried out by the Apostles, the priests and the servants in every generation.

From the spirituality of the rite of the Divine Liturgy, the Church ordained that the first prayer in the Liturgy of the Faithful is the Prayer of Reconciliation, to declare to us and remind us of the reconciliation that Christ accomplished by the sacrifice of His body, so that we may remain in this reconciliation by Communion on the one hand and by a life of repentance and holiness on the other.

entries.section: (3) Reconciling people with God so that they live for His love

paragraphs.text: The Apostles and servants, in their preaching of Christ, are ambassadors for God, when they exhort people and call them to believe in Him and accept reconciliation with Him. This does not happen only when proclaiming to unbelievers, but also to believers, by their accepting reconciliation when they sin and being reconciled in the Sacrament of repentance and confession, and then partaking of the Holy Mysteries, so that they are united with God.
How great is the humility of God, who seeks reconciliation with His creation that is disobedient and rejects Him.

May you seek with love to be reconciled with the one who wrongs you, and rather with the one whom you have wronged, so that you may win everyone, even if you endure some reproach or rebuke from the other. And be confident that strength is love, forgiveness and the pursuit of reconciliation, so you will receive God's blessing and the love of others and live in peace.

entries.section: (3) Reconciling people with God so that they live for His love

paragraphs.text: God declares His inexpressible love in His Son Jesus Christ, the holy and righteous, as He said of Himself to the multitudes, "Which of you convinceth me of sin?" (Jn 8:46), in that He made Him, by His bearing our sins on the cross, stained with sin because of His love for us. Whoever looks at Him as He is crucified sees Him tortured and dying as a sinner, despite His perfect righteousness. And by Christ's death for us, we have become righteous and pure from sin through the Sacrament of Baptism, and whoever sees us sees the righteousness of God in us through our pure nature that comes out of the baptismal font. Paul's sincerity and forbearance toward the Corinthians

entries.section: (1) Paul's sincerity and labor in the ministry

paragraphs.text: Paul, with the rest of the Apostles and servants, received the grace of working together with God to preach in His name, and this is the greatest honor a person can receive. Since his aim is to preach the grace of Christ that renews man through the Holy Sacraments, he asks the Corinthians not to receive this grace in vain, that is, to turn back from their sins and not be slothful in works of righteousness and goodness.

entries.section: (1) Paul's sincerity and labor in the ministry

paragraphs.text: Paul urges the Corinthians to accept the faith without delay or hesitation, and he draws on the words of Isaiah in (Isa 49:8) to affirm to them the importance of seizing the opportunity by accepting the faith and thereby enjoying the work of God's grace in them.

entries.section: (1) Paul's sincerity and labor in the ministry

paragraphs.text: In Paul's preaching of Christ, he was careful that no one should find fault with him, be offended because of him, and reject the faith. So he offered his love to all, endured many labors, and was careful in his conduct so that his ministry would be pure and draw as many as possible to Christ, such as his readiness not to eat meat if this could cause one of the weak believers to stumble (1 Cor 8:13).

entries.section: (1) Paul's sincerity and labor in the ministry

paragraphs.text: St. Paul and his companions present the proof of their sincerity in the ministry and their love, that they may win all souls, and this proof is patience in enduring sufferings. He presents nine of them here, the first three of which any Christian may be exposed to, namely:
Distresses: sufferings that are hard to bear.
Necessities: deprivation of the things necessary for life, such as food or drink.
Afflictions: sufferings that hem a person in, so that he cannot escape from them.
Then he speaks of three sufferings to which he himself was exposed, namely:
Stripes: Paul was beaten eight times, five by the Jews and three by the Romans (ch. 11:

24, 25). In imprisonments: Paul was thrown into prison many times, as at Philippi (Acts 16:23), Jerusalem (Acts 22:24) and Rome (Acts 28:16). Tumults: Paul was exposed to the agitation of crowds against him, and even attempts to kill him many times, as at Antioch of Pisidia (Acts 13:50), Lystra (Acts 14:19) and Jerusalem (Acts 21:30). Finally he speaks of three voluntary sufferings which the spiritually striving person takes upon himself, namely: Labors: this includes all the labors of spiritual striving and service.
Watchings: this means keeping vigil in prayer and service and enduring various sufferings.

Fastings: so that God may intervene in the life of the one who strives spiritually and in his service, whether they are communal fasts of the whole Church or individual fasts that the striving person adds to the general fasts.

entries.section: (1) Paul's sincerity and labor in the ministry

paragraphs.text: St. Paul continues to declare his sincerity in the ministry, not only by enduring sufferings but also through virtues, and he tells us of nine of them, namely:
By pureness: that is, purity of heart and conduct.
By knowledge: knowledge of God and His work in the Church and the eternal Kingdom.
By longsuffering: when a person is filled with spiritual knowledge, he is longsuffering toward others and endures sufferings for God's sake.
By kindness: likewise he shows his love and tenderness toward others.
By the Holy Ghost: He supports the servant with many gifts and virtues.
By love unfeigned: the love offered to others becomes pure, without any ulterior purpose.
By the word of truth: the truth is God, so we proclaim Him in all our speech with others.
By the power of God: which supports the servants and the believers.

By the armour of righteousness on the right hand and on the left: works of righteousness are strong like armor on the right hand, that is, the various virtues, or on the left, that is, cutting off evil and sins.

entries.section: (1) Paul's sincerity and labor in the ministry

paragraphs.text: Finally St. Paul shows the steadfastness of his love for God in all circumstances, in nine situations, namely:
By honour and dishonour: he continues in his love and service whether he receives honor from people or they insult and despise him.
By evil report and good report: a good reputation, the testimony of people and their praise of him, or on the contrary their condemnation and contempt of him and the spreading of slander against him.

As deceivers, and yet true: the Apostles and servants bear being accused of error and false teachings although their words are the truth and honesty that ought to be followed, because it is the right faith.

As unknown, and yet well known: people may neglect us and consider us fools, and we lose every position and standing among people. But we are confident that we are known to God and among the believers in the Church, who care to hear the word of God.
As dying, and behold, we live: the Apostles are often exposed to death, but God rescues them so that they live and continue their preaching.

As chastened, and not killed: they endure many sufferings as though they were chastisement for their sins, although they are a loving fellowship in the cross of Christ, but God rescues them from death and heals them of their wounds.

As sorrowful, yet alway rejoicing: from the multitude of sufferings, sorrow appears on the Apostles, but in truth they are in inward peace and joy in the work of God, who rescues them and makes them feel His presence with them and gives them to enjoy inexpressible comforts.

As poor, yet making many rich: for the sake of Christ the Apostles appear in need and poverty in material things although they are rich in what is more important, which is the spiritual blessings that they pour out on others from God. As having nothing, and yet possessing all things: the Apostles appear as though they own nothing in the world and need everything, although they possess everything, that is, Christ, who satisfies them.

Do not be troubled if afflictions come upon you or people neglect you or you are exposed to various abuses, for all these are external. Only hold fast to God and seek Him with persistence, and you will experience Him and feel His presence with you and your heart will rejoice, so that you are not shaken by any suffering.

entries.section: (2) Paul's love and forbearance toward the Corinthians

paragraphs.text: Our mouth is open: continuing to exhort and teach them.
Our heart is enlarged: filled with love, forgiveness and fatherhood.
Paul was not affected by the wrongs some of the Corinthians did to him when they followed false teachers and troubled him, but he continued to exhort them and love them, forgiving all their faults.

entries.section: (2) Paul's love and forbearance toward the Corinthians

paragraphs.text: Ye are not straitened in us: that is, our hearts are open in love to you and have not been constrained by your wrongs. Straitened in your own bowels: you have created a constraint within yourselves by your siding against us, your following false teachers and your wronging us.
The Apostle declares his love for the Corinthians and assures them that he was not affected by the evil that is in their hearts toward him.

entries.section: (2) Paul's love and forbearance toward the Corinthians

paragraphs.text: Now for a recompense in the same: as a result of my love toward you.
As unto my children: because he loves them as a father, since he begot them as children of Christ by his preaching among them.
Paul calls the Corinthians to abandon the evil in their hearts toward him, and to love him as he loves them, because he is their father and seeks their salvation.

When others wrong you, have pity on them, because sin is weakness. In this way the evil within them becomes limited until you put an end to it by your prayers and your love. That is, keep your heart filled with love toward everyone, like your Christ who died for the disobedient, and be confident that He will rejoice in you and support you.

(3) Not mingling with the wicked (vv. 14-18 - ch. 7:1) 14 "Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers: for what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness? 15 And what concord hath Christ with Belial? or what part hath he that believeth with an infidel? 16 And what agreement hath the temple of God with idols? for ye are the temple of the living God; as God hath said, I will dwell in them, and walk in them; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people. 17 Wherefore come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing; and I will receive you, 18 And will be a Father unto you, and ye shall be my sons and daughters, saith the Lord Almighty. Ch. 7:1 Having therefore these promises, dearly beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from all filthiness of the flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God."

entries.section: (2) Paul's love and forbearance toward the Corinthians

paragraphs.text: Yoke: a crossbeam placed on the necks of two animals to join them together, with a perpendicular beam attached to its middle, at the end of which is the farming implement such as the plow.

The Law of Moses decreed that a yoke should not be placed on two animals of different kinds, because the strength of one differs from the other, so they cannot pull the farming implement in a balanced way. The spiritual purpose of this law was that believers should not mingle with unbelievers.

And here St. Paul confirms this truth, warning the believers not to mingle with unbelievers and the wicked at idol-worship feasts or any celebrations not fitting for the children of God, so that they do not share with them in doing evil. He gives as the reason that there can be no mixture between sin and righteousness because they are repugnant to each other, and likewise between light and darkness because they are opposites. Likewise the conduct and life of the children of God cannot agree and share with the wicked in their wickedness.

entries.section: (2) Paul's love and forbearance toward the Corinthians

paragraphs.text: Belial: a Hebrew name meaning "wicked," by which Satan is meant.

The Apostle affirms the necessity of believers' not mingling with unbelievers, just as there can be no agreement between the leader of each party, that is, Christ and Satan. Likewise the portion and reward of each party differ: the believers have the Kingdom of Heaven, while the unbelievers who reject Christ have eternal torment.

entries.section: (2) Paul's love and forbearance toward the Corinthians

paragraphs.text: The Apostle argues for the necessity of believers' not mingling with pagan unbelievers by saying that believers are the temple of God, set apart for His worship, which is completely different from what is set apart for the worship of idols, that is, the wicked unbelievers, because the believer, by his prayers, worship and service, becomes a temple of God. The Apostle confirmed his words with verses from the Holy Bible, that the children of God are temples for Him in which He dwells and walks among them (1 Cor 3:16), and likewise He is their God whom they worship, and He takes them as a people of His own, as He said in (Jer 31:33).

entries.section: (2) Paul's love and forbearance toward the Corinthians

paragraphs.text: Paul relies on the word of God in Isaiah (Isa 52:11), and calls the believers in Corinth to keep away from unbelievers and reject their evil works and not be present in their assemblies filled with sin; then God receives them as sons and rejoices in them.

entries.section: (2) Paul's love and forbearance toward the Corinthians

paragraphs.text: Paul also borrows God's word to David in (2 Sam 7:14) to affirm God's love for the believers who separate themselves from the wicked and the unbelievers, by granting them His fatherhood and caring for them as His children.

Let your heart be open in love to everyone, but be careful to preserve your purity by keeping away from mingling with the wicked. You will meet the people of the world and deal with them well in all areas of life and love them and serve them, but take care that their strange thoughts do not enter your heart, so that you always live by the word of God and His commandments.

entries.section: (2) Paul's love and forbearance toward the Corinthians

paragraphs.text: Because we enjoy God's fatherhood and His promises to care for us and work in us by His grace, we must respond to this love with repentance and confession, to cut off all bodily and spiritual desires. Then we look to the Day of Judgment, so we fear God and strive toward holiness, to partake of the Holy Mysteries, to do good and to grow in the virtues. Titus reassures Paul about the repentance of the Corinthians

entries.section: (1) The news of the Corinthians comforts Paul

paragraphs.text: Receive us: as apostles and servants of Christ, and accordingly receive our teachings, that is, the commandments of God.

We have wronged no man: we were not hasty in judging anyone. Perhaps some false teachers accused him of haste in judging the sinner of Corinth who committed fornication with his father's wife, whom he cut off from the Church for a period. We have corrupted no man: we have not caused anyone to stumble by our teachings and led him away from the truth.
We have defrauded no man: we had no material purpose, nor did we exploit anyone's money and possessions, as the false teachers did.
St. Paul asks them to receive him so that they may receive his teachings, because he dealt with them well, in all love and without personal purpose, and caused no one to stumble.

entries.section: (1) The news of the Corinthians comforts Paul

paragraphs.text: He calls them to receive God's teachings from their mouths, because they have not wronged them or exploited them. In clearing himself the Apostle did not intend to condemn the Corinthians, but that no one should doubt him, so that they would receive his teachings, and he affirms the depth of his love for them by saying that they are in his heart, that is, that they are his children and a part of him, because they are all members of one body, which is the Church; he rejoices in their joy and grieves in their grief.
To die and live with you: if you suffer and endure afflictions that approach death, we grieve for you and almost die with you.
To live with you: when you rejoice and live with God, we also are enthusiastic and rejoice.

entries.section: (1) The news of the Corinthians comforts Paul

paragraphs.text: The Apostle shows that he did not intend to condemn them, in that he:
1- Trusts in their love and their faith.
2- Boasts of them, and therefore is not inclined to blame them.
3- When Paul passed through afflictions and heard their good news, he was greatly comforted and rejoiced.

entries.section: (1) The news of the Corinthians comforts Paul

paragraphs.text: Paul explained the afflictions he passed through in Macedonia in Greece, and the afflictions are divided into two kinds:
1- Quarrels and oppositions from the Jews and the Gentiles to his preaching of Christ.

2- His anxiety about the faith of the believers in Macedonia and the surrounding countries because of the doubts and oppositions of the false teachers and the agitation of the wicked against the Church.

entries.section: (1) The news of the Corinthians comforts Paul

paragraphs.text: Paul declares God's tenderness toward His children who humble themselves before Him in prayers of lowliness, as Paul and those with him did, so God encouraged them with the news that Titus brought from Corinth, because Paul had sent him to them to reassure himself about them and to encourage them.

entries.section: (1) The news of the Corinthians comforts Paul

paragraphs.text: Paul rejoiced at seeing Titus, his beloved son. He was also comforted in his afflictions by the news Titus brought him from the Corinthians, which includes:
1- Their earnest desire: toward Paul, with great love.
2- Their mourning: that is, repentance with weeping over their sins.
3- Their fervent mind: for life with God and for establishing Paul's authority as a responsible bishop.
Thus what Titus reported was the cause of Paul's comfort during his sufferings in Macedonia.

Offer good, encouraging words to everyone you meet, and you will lighten his pain and support him in his afflictions, and be confident that you will be the first to be comforted and to rejoice when you do this, as a reward from God.

entries.section: (2) Paul's joy at the repentance of the Corinthians

paragraphs.text: Here Paul speaks of his rebuke of the Corinthians in his first epistle because of the fornicator, as mentioned in its fifth chapter. This grieved them and stirred their feelings to repentance, so Paul meant what he said, or what God revealed to him and he wrote in the epistle. He did not regret that he grieved them for a time, as he says, "but for a season," because this sorrow led to their salvation and their keeping away from sins. Although his feelings as a father were affected and he regretted that he had grieved them, out of tender human feelings, he held fast to the word of God and declared it to them, because the most important thing is that they repent, even if his heart as a father suffered because of their sorrow. This shows the tenderness of Paul's feelings and his fatherhood.

entries.section: (2) Paul's joy at the repentance of the Corinthians

paragraphs.text: That ye might receive damage by us in nothing: you lose nothing because of our teaching, but rather gain repentance.

Joy filled Paul's heart, not because of the Corinthians' sorrow, but because their sorrow turned into repentance. This sorrow is "after a godly manner," to distinguish it from sorrow over the loss of some material things. Thus by their sorrow and repentance they lost nothing, but received God's forgiveness and blessing.

entries.section: (2) Paul's joy at the repentance of the Corinthians

paragraphs.text: Paul makes clear the difference between holy sorrow, that is, sorrow over the act of sin, which produces repentance and trust in God's forgiveness in the Sacrament of repentance and confession, and an inclination to a new beginning, so that the person holds fast to repentance and does not regret this sorrow, because it is the way to life with God and to salvation. In contrast, we find that sorrow over the loss of material things reveals man's attachment to these desires, and this is sin, and the wages of sin is eternal death if a person persists in it.

entries.section: (2) Paul's joy at the repentance of the Corinthians

paragraphs.text: Here Paul shows the results of the repentance of the Corinthians, for the sorrow of repentance moved them to:

Carefulness: spiritual striving in cutting off sin and clinging to God in prayers and fasts. Clearing of yourselves: they rejected the sin of the fornicator and rejected their own sins in order to forsake them and live for God. Indignation: distress over their sins that separate them from God.
Fear: of God, so that they live before Him in purity.
Vehement desire: for the pure life with God and for acquiring the various virtues.
Revenge: on the fornicator, by cutting him off until he repents, and the discipline of everyone who violates God's commandments so that the Church remains pure.
Thus by their repentance they declared their submission to God, so they received His forgiveness and became innocent. This is the great work of repentance.

entries.section: (2) Paul's joy at the repentance of the Corinthians

paragraphs.text: He that had done the wrong: the young man who committed fornication with his father's wife.

He that suffered wrong: the father whose son committed fornication with his wife, for the father was still alive. Our care for you: our love for you, that you may live pure and God's wrath may not come upon you. Paul shows his concern that the Church of Corinth live in purity. What moved him in cutting off the fornicator was not a personal grievance against him or a special pity for the father, whose wife the young man committed fornication with, but what moved him was his love for righteousness and the purity in which God wants the Church to live.

entries.section: (2) Paul's joy at the repentance of the Corinthians

paragraphs.text: Paul declares the rest of his heart because of the comfort of the Corinthians and the rest that resulted from their repentance, and the Apostle's comfort increased because of the joy of Titus, his son and friend whom he trusts, because he saw with his own eyes their repentance and their spiritual conduct, so he was at rest about their spiritual life and put Paul's mind at ease, and Paul rejoiced more because the whole Church of Corinth lived in true repentance.

entries.section: (2) Paul's joy at the repentance of the Corinthians

paragraphs.text: Paul took care to teach the Corinthians the whole truth, and not as the false teachers cast doubt on Paul's teachings for them. Paul also boasted of the virtues of the Corinthians before Titus before sending him to them. When Titus went to them, he was assured of their repentance and good conduct and that their works matched Paul's praise of them.

entries.section: (2) Paul's joy at the repentance of the Corinthians

paragraphs.text: Titus's love for the Corinthians increased after he visited them, because of their obedience to the word of God and their welcome and reverence toward him.

entries.section: (2) Paul's joy at the repentance of the Corinthians

paragraphs.text: Paul sums up his feelings toward the Corinthians, which are joy in them because of his confidence in them, since their repentance and obedience have become clear and strong.
Accept the advice or rebuke of others, especially your father of confession and your spiritual guide, for this is your medicine that saves you from your sins.
Collecting gifts from Corinth for the needy in Jerusalem

entries.section: (1) The generosity of the gifts of the Macedonians

paragraphs.text: The churches of Macedonia: in northern Greece, and among their most famous churches are Philippi and Thessalonica.

Paul wrote to the Corinthians in the first epistle, calling them to collect alms for the needs of the poor believers in Jerusalem. Now he encourages them to give by mentioning the churches of Macedonia and their concern in collecting donations for the needy in Jerusalem.

entries.section: (1) The generosity of the gifts of the Macedonians

paragraphs.text: The gifts of the Macedonians were distinguished not by their abundance, but rather because they came from believers who suffered from material poverty but enjoyed abundant and great spiritual joy, so they gave out of their need beyond what was expected of them, because of their love for Christ and their concern for the needy in Jerusalem.

entries.section: (1) The generosity of the gifts of the Macedonians

paragraphs.text: Here Paul declares two important facts about the gifts of the churches of Macedonia, namely:
1- That they gave beyond their ability, for they are poor and needy, yet they gave out of their need.
2- Of their own accord, and not by orders from Paul or insistence from him, contrary to what happened in Corinth, so they were distinguished by their delicate sensitivity to the needy.

entries.section: (1) The generosity of the gifts of the Macedonians

paragraphs.text: Here Paul shows two new virtues in the gifts of the Macedonians:
1- Their urging Paul to accept their gifts, for their love for the needy was strong, and their poverty did not prevent them from this.

2- Their humility, for they begged him not to refuse their gifts, so that they might enjoy the fellowship of love with their brethren in the body of Christ, that is, the Church, counting their sharing in the ministry of giving as a grace they did not deserve.

entries.section: (1) The generosity of the gifts of the Macedonians

paragraphs.text: The fifth virtue in the giving of the Macedonians is their readiness to give all they had, even themselves. This is after the example of what Christ did, for He was not content with healing the sick and feeding the multitudes, but gave Himself on the cross for our salvation.

entries.section: (1) The generosity of the gifts of the Macedonians

paragraphs.text: As the believers in Macedonia were moved to give to the needy in Jerusalem, Paul thought it good that the Corinthians share in this grace, that is, the ministry of giving. Titus had spoken to them about it when he was with them, and then visited them afterward and collected these gifts.

Any gift you give to the needy, whether materially, or in the soul by helping a poor person, visiting a sick person or caring for a person who suffers from psychological troubles, is a grace to you because you offer it to Christ, who rejoices greatly in your giving and rewards you with many blessings on earth and in heaven.

entries.section: (2) Encouraging the Corinthians to give
