paragraphs.text: Paul praises the Corinthians for their concern to grow in the virtues, and he gave examples of them: Faith: in Christ and His work in them.
Utterance: speaking about spiritual matters and supporting and encouraging others.
Knowledge: the knowledge of God and the Church and everything in it.
Diligence: in repentance and rejecting sins, and also in acquiring the virtues.
Your love to us: in obeying Paul and esteeming his words and teachings.
Then he gently asks them to take care to grow in this grace, that is, the virtue of giving.

entries.section: (2) Encouraging the Corinthians to give

paragraphs.text: The Apostle shows that giving comes from love and sensitivity to others, and not merely obeying orders issued by Paul. He explained that he directs their attention to the concern of the Macedonians for giving, and then expects, as a result of their love and sincerity, that they also will give as much as they are able.

entries.section: (2) Encouraging the Corinthians to give

paragraphs.text: The Apostle offers a second encouragement to the Corinthians to give, after encouraging them with the giving of the Macedonians, and it is the greatest encouragement, because it is Christ Himself, who gave up everything by His Incarnation and was born in the humblest place, the manger, and lived in poverty in order to redeem us and satisfy us and enrich us by His gift to us. For He took what is ours and gave us what is His, as we say in the Friday Praise, so that we became partakers of the divine nature and heirs of the Kingdom. This is thus a motive for us to give up our comfort and care for and give to the needy. Christ gave up everything, while we give up a little of material things to give even the bare necessities to the needy. The devil prevails against them and makes them fall into sin, or shows their physical weakness before the wicked, but God strengthens them and heals them and raises them up again with power, so that they continue their striving and their ministry.

entries.section: (2) Encouraging the Corinthians to give

paragraphs.text: In this matter: collecting gifts for the needy in Jerusalem.
For this: the opinion and guidance that Paul gives about collecting the gifts.

Paul commends the Corinthians that they thought of collecting gifts for their needy brethren in Judea, and when the Macedonians heard of this they were moved and collected gifts. So Paul encourages the Corinthians to carry out what they thought of, as the Macedonians collected. And he gives them guidance in collecting the gifts, which he mentions in the following verses.

entries.section: (2) Encouraging the Corinthians to give

paragraphs.text: The doing: collecting the gifts.
Out of that which ye have: according to your ability.

The Apostle encourages the Corinthians to complete their intention to donate to the needy. They should not be content with their desire and willingness to give, but complete this with diligence, that is, an actual collection of the gifts, according to each one's ability and his financial and spiritual capacity.

entries.section: (2) Encouraging the Corinthians to give

paragraphs.text: The readiness: collecting the gifts.

The Apostle confirms what was said in the previous verse, that the collection is to be according to each one's ability. So let no one demand of himself more than his ability, for God values the gift according to the love and self-sacrifice of the giver and not the quantity of the gift.

entries.section: (2) Encouraging the Corinthians to give

paragraphs.text: The Apostle completes the idea mentioned in the two preceding verses, which is that he does not mean that they should give up and give beyond their ability, so that they become poor and in distress for the ease of others. That is a high spiritual level, but it is enough that they give up a little so that others may have some relief like them.

entries.section: (2) Encouraging the Corinthians to give

paragraphs.text: Your abundance a supply for their want: the material gifts of the Corinthians that meet the needs of the needy in Jerusalem.

Their abundance also may be a supply for your want: the Apostles and servants whom the Church of Jerusalem sent to preach to the Gentiles, who meet their spiritual needs and fill them with Christ like the believers in Jerusalem.

Here the Apostle declares a truth, which is that when the churches of the Gentiles give to the needy in Judea, they at the same time receive spiritual gifts, that is, the preaching of Christ and the ministry and pastoral care that flow from Jerusalem. Each party gives some of what it has, the first giving material things and the second giving spiritual things, but not at anyone's expense or beyond anyone's ability. Whoever gives material or spiritual things gives some of what he has and not all that he has. Thus there is equality, that is, both parties are satisfied spiritually and materially as a result of the other's giving.

entries.section: (2) Encouraging the Corinthians to give

paragraphs.text: Paul confirms his words about equality among all by what happened with the children of Israel in the wilderness of Sinai when the manna fell on the ground around their tents and they went out to gather it every morning (Ex 16:18). The strong, who gathered much, took only what he needed and gave the rest to the weak, and the physically weak, who gathered little, took from the strong, so that everyone came out with a certain measure, which was a measure among the children of Israel called the omer, so everyone was satisfied and no one kept any of the manna until the next day, because it spoiled if it was kept overnight.

As Paul was gentle and encouraging to the Corinthians in giving, may you, when you ask someone for something, or direct him to correct some mistake, begin your words with praise and then encourage him gently, so that you win his love and reach what you want.

entries.section: (3) Paul's testimony about those sent to collect the gifts

paragraphs.text: Care: concern for collecting the gifts.
The same: like Paul's concern.
Paul thanks God, who put the concern for collecting the gifts into the heart of Titus as into the heart of Paul, to collect them from the Corinthians, for God is the One who moves all virtues in us.

entries.section: (3) Paul's testimony about those sent to collect the gifts

paragraphs.text: The exhortation: Paul asked Titus to go to Corinth to collect the donations.
Of his own accord: he was intending to go to Corinth, so he responded at once to Paul's request to him to do so.
Paul shows Titus's concern and diligence in collecting the gifts, so that he accepted to go to Corinth as soon as Paul asked him to.

entries.section: (3) Paul's testimony about those sent to collect the gifts

paragraphs.text: In the gospel: that is, in the preaching.

Paul sent with Titus one of the servants who assisted him to help in collecting the gifts, and describes this servant as known and praised in all the churches of Macedonia in which he preached. He did not specify the identity of this servant, but he was most likely Luke, who accompanied Paul on most of his journeys, as the Book of Acts testifies.

entries.section: (3) Paul's testimony about those sent to collect the gifts

paragraphs.text: This grace which is administered by us: collecting the donations that Paul commanded, in the collection of which his two assistants Titus and Luke shared.
The glory of the same Lord: Christ, in whom we all believe and whom we all worship, for these gifts glorify Him because they declare the love of His children for one another.
Your readiness of mind: your concern and love in offering the gifts.

Paul affirms and continues his praise of Luke, who was chosen to perform this ministry, that is, collecting the gifts, so that God may be glorified and their love for their brethren shown. Paul offers all this praise so that the Corinthians may trust Luke and give him their money.

entries.section: (3) Paul's testimony about those sent to collect the gifts

paragraphs.text: Abundance: the greatness and largeness of the sum collected.
Administered: the ministry of collecting the gifts.

We see Paul's exactness in his caution in collecting the gifts, because the sum collected was large, so that no one would doubt him or one of his companions, which would lead them to doubt the teachings of Christ that he proclaims; he was careful to send trustworthy people to collect the gifts.

entries.section: (3) Paul's testimony about those sent to collect the gifts

paragraphs.text: Paul did not collect the gifts himself and give them to the needy in Jerusalem, so that no one would suspect him. So he arranged for delegates on his behalf to collect the donations, as well as delegates from the people of the countries, so that all the people would be assured that their gifts were in faithful hands, and thus no one would stumble.

entries.section: (3) Paul's testimony about those sent to collect the gifts

paragraphs.text: Paul sent with Titus and Luke a third servant who was distinguished by his concern and diligence in the ministry, and was even enthusiastic about the ministry of collecting gifts from the Corinthians because of his confidence in their love and self-giving, so he came forward to Paul wishing to share in this ministry. He was one of Paul's companions to Jerusalem and was most likely Tychicus (Acts 20:4).

entries.section: (3) Paul's testimony about those sent to collect the gifts

paragraphs.text: Paul sums up his recommendation and testimony about those sent to collect the gifts from the Corinthians. They are Titus, whom he describes as his partner in the ministry and preaching, and the two brethren accompanying Titus, who are most likely Luke and Tychicus, whom he describes as messengers of the churches of the Gentiles and delegates for them in collecting the donations and delivering them to Jerusalem to declare the glory of Christ in the love of the believers for one another.

entries.section: (3) Paul's testimony about those sent to collect the gifts

paragraphs.text: Shew ye to them: show your love to these three delegates in the generosity of your giving. Before the churches: considering these messengers as delegates of the churches of Macedonia, which had gone ahead and collected for the needy, so show them your love also in your gifts.
The proof of your love: the evidence of your love.
Of our boasting on your behalf: considering that Paul is their apostle and they are his children, their love and their giving gladden him and he boasts of it.
Finally Paul encourages them to be generous in giving for the sake of God and His three servants who will collect the donations, and so that he also may rejoice and boast in their love.

It is good that your heart be pure before God, but care also for people's feelings, so do not cause anyone to stumble, even unintentionally. And care to draw everyone by your love for Christ, and let us not forget to provide for honest things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men (v. 21). Attention to generous giving with cheerfulness

entries.section: (1) Paul urges the Corinthians to give

paragraphs.text: The ministering: collecting gifts for the poor.

The saints: those sanctified in Christ, that is, the believers, and he means the poor Christians in Jerusalem. This is different from the title we give to those who have reached a high degree in the spiritual life, whom we call saints. Superfluous: excessive talk.

Paul encourages the Corinthians to collect gifts for the poor of Jerusalem, and affirms their concern for this, and in a gentle manner says that his words are superfluous but he means them only as a reminder.

entries.section: (1) Paul urges the Corinthians to give

paragraphs.text: Your forwardness of mind: your concern to offer gifts for the poor.
They of Macedonia: the believers in the northern part of Greece.
Achaia: the southern part of Greece, whose capital is Corinth, and here he means the believers in Corinth.

Paul commends the Christians in Corinth, because their concern for collecting donations encouraged the other churches to do so, although they had not yet collected anything, but when they heard last year of this need they declared their readiness to take part in it. This is a gentle approach by Paul when urging them to collect gifts, to commend them first, since he found in them a heartfelt concern, even if they had not expressed it by an actual collection of gifts.

entries.section: (1) Paul urges the Corinthians to give

paragraphs.text: The brethren: Titus and his two companions.

The boldness of boasting: Paul's boldness in boasting of the Corinthians in their concern for collecting the gifts. Paul sent Titus and the servants with him to encourage the Church of Corinth and collect the donations, and he expects some believers from Macedonia to accompany him, so he encourages them by this epistle to collect the gifts so that his boasting of their concern in this matter may be justified, and so that they do not put him to shame, and put themselves to shame, if they were slack and were content with readiness in words and did nothing.

entries.section: (1) Paul urges the Corinthians to give

paragraphs.text: Paul sent Titus and his two companions to collect the donations before he himself arrived with some Christians from the churches of Macedonia, for it was the custom that some believers accompanied him on his journeys, so that when he arrived the collection would be complete. He calls these gifts a blessing, not only for the one who receives but also for the one who gives, because he gave to Christ. His intention in this was that the Corinthians should not fall short, having collected little and not completed the whole collection, and do it in his presence before the Macedonians, so that their shortcoming and stinginess would appear. So he wants the collection to be completed by Titus before he arrives with the Macedonians.
When you ask something of someone or reproach him for some mistake, may you begin your words with praise, for this makes the other ready to accept your words and even to rejoice in them.

entries.section: (2) Giving generously and cheerfully

paragraphs.text: Paul calls the Corinthians to give generously, drawing on what happens in farming. He who sows few seeds reaps a small harvest from them, but he who sows bountifully, that is, with abundance of seed, reaps a large harvest. Likewise he who gives little to the needy, God grants him few blessings in his life, but he who gives generously, God's blessings to him are many.

entries.section: (2) Giving generously and cheerfully

paragraphs.text: Grudgingly: he gives but is troubled when he gives, because he loves money and is attached to it.
Of necessity: he is embarrassed before the one who asks him, or ashamed before those around him, so he gives but not out of love.

Here the Apostle calls believers to give cheerfully, for the gift of each one must be given with love so that God's heart may rejoice. Paul cited a verse with this meaning from the Book of Proverbs (Prov 22:9) as in the Septuagint.

entries.section: (2) Giving generously and cheerfully

paragraphs.text: The Apostle promises the one who gives that God will reward him with many graces and provide for his material needs in everything and at every time, that is, always. And when his material needs are supplied, he is free to care for spiritual growth and for increasing works of goodness. The Church has taken up this verse in the Divine Liturgy in the Litany of the Plants, the Airs of Heaven and the Waters of the Rivers.

entries.section: (2) Giving generously and cheerfully

paragraphs.text: The Apostle affirms his words about God's blessings to the one who gives, for He helps him so that he keeps giving throughout his life and therefore lives in righteousness, not only on earth but also in the Kingdom forever. He cited the Book of Psalms (Ps 112:9).

entries.section: (2) Giving generously and cheerfully

paragraphs.text: The Apostle reassures those who give that they will not become poor and needy, because God, who gives the whole world, both seed to the farmer so that he may sow it and food to the hungry, is Himself able to give to those who give to the needy not only material gifts but also righteousness and the spiritual life with Him.

entries.section: (2) Giving generously and cheerfully

paragraphs.text: Paul shows that God's gifts to those who give generously are sufficient for them and enrich them, and this makes Paul and all the believers thank God: 1- for His gifts to the one who gives; 2- that He put into the heart of the one who gives a concern for others; 3- for supplying the needs of the needy.

entries.section: (2) Giving generously and cheerfully

paragraphs.text: The administration of this service: carrying out the collection of the gifts.
Here Paul affirms that collecting the gifts not only supplies the needs of the poor in Jerusalem but also increases prayers of thanksgiving to God, so the life of the believers grows.

entries.section: (2) Giving generously and cheerfully

paragraphs.text: They: the poor in Jerusalem.
The experiment of this ministration: when they receive the gifts from the Corinthians.
Your professed subjection: your obedience, you believers who confess Christ.
The Apostle shows the feelings of the believers in Jerusalem when they receive these gifts, so they thank God for two things:
1- The existence of many believers in the world who obey the Gospel and offer gifts out of love for God.
2- The many gifts which they receive in abundance.

entries.section: (2) Giving generously and cheerfully

paragraphs.text: The Apostle continues the feelings of the believers in Jerusalem when they receive the gifts, and they do two things:
1- They pray for you, believers of Corinth.
2- They long to see them, as they feel their fellowship with them in the body of Christ, that is, the one Church.

entries.section: (2) Giving generously and cheerfully

paragraphs.text: Finally Paul thanks God for His grace, which is first faith in Christ and the work of the Holy Spirit, who stirs up love in the hearts of the believers so that they give gifts to the needy.
If you look at God's gifts to you, given generously and with fatherly love, your heart will be moved to care for everyone around you, and you will give with joy and give generously.
The authority of St. Paul the Apostle

entries.section: (1) Paul's authority over those who oppose him

paragraphs.text: St. Paul speaks with meekness like the meek Christ, and says to the Corinthians that he was an ordinary, weak man when he preached to them, and they received his gentle words, but now in the epistle he appears strong and speaks with authority. The truth is that Paul was not weak, but he humbled himself in meekness during his preaching, and then those who oppose him rose up against him, provoking him to come among them, and they interpreted his delay in coming as fear and weakness to face them, although it is not so. As a bishop and spiritual head over them he has his authority, whether among them or when he sends them an epistle, and the concerns of the ministry are what keep him from coming.

entries.section: (1) Paul's authority over those who oppose him

paragraphs.text: Be bold: act with authority and severity.
Some: the false teachers who oppose Paul.
As if we walked according to the flesh: acting according to the evil desires of the flesh and not as spiritual people.

Paul wishes that when he comes to Corinth he will not find opposition and errors from the false teachers who influence the believers, so that he will not be compelled to use his spiritual authority to punish the offenders, even if those who oppose him interpret these actions of his as mistaken human behavior, that is, that he became angry and out of his anger issues commands and punishments.

entries.section: (1) Paul's authority over those who oppose him

paragraphs.text: Paul declares that although he is a man who lives in the flesh, that is, eats and drinks and sleeps like the rest of human beings, he does not wage war in his spiritual striving and ministry in a human way, that is, with passions and desires and pride, but walks in a spiritual way.

entries.section: (1) Paul's authority over those who oppose him

paragraphs.text: Paul declares that the weapons with which he fights are spiritual and not carnal, those he mentioned in (Eph 6:11-16), and they are strong weapons able to pull down the strongholds of evil in which the people who oppose the work of God walk.

entries.section: (1) Paul's authority over those who oppose him

paragraphs.text: Every high thing: in ancient times they built strongholds on high places. Here the Apostle likens the pride of those who oppose to these high strongholds.
Every thought: every person.

Paul speaks with confidence in God and in his spiritual weapons, that they are able to remove the evil imaginations that those who oppose stir up in the midst of the Church to disturb it, and to overcome their pride and draw souls to faith and obedience to the commandments of Christ, so that they become captive to His love.

entries.section: (1) Paul's authority over those who oppose him

paragraphs.text: The Apostle reassures the believers in Corinth that if they submit to him in the obedience of children, they need not be troubled by those who oppose, who cause problems within the Church, for he is able by the power of God to avenge, that is, to punish them in order to stop their evils and so that they repent.

Be gentle and show your love to others, but do not give up the truth; rather proclaim it. Also, if you have responsibility as a parent or a superior, use your authority to prevent evil for God's sake, and not as human anger or for private purposes.

entries.section: (2) Paul's authority from God

paragraphs.text: Paul addresses those who oppose and says to them, if you look at me as a weak man when I was present with you, I declare to you that if you believe in Christ, be confident that I have the same faith and power. For some of them claimed distinction because they had seen Christ in the flesh, or because of a distant bodily kinship with Jesus.

entries.section: (2) Paul's authority from God

paragraphs.text: In the previous verse, Paul showed that he is no less in his faith in Christ than those who oppose him in the Church of Corinth. Here he declares his distinction from them by his authority as head and the one responsible for the Church, and his boasting and holding to this authority is for the edification of the Church and not for its destruction like these who oppose. He is not ashamed to declare this authority because he received it from Christ when He called him, and he uses it for His glory.

entries.section: (2) Paul's authority from God

paragraphs.text: Here Paul repels the charge of these who oppose him, that he frightens the believers in Corinth by his epistles. The truth is that what he says is not a threat but real authority from God that he can use if these who oppose persist in their evil.

entries.section: (2) Paul's authority from God

paragraphs.text: Paul denounces the words of those who oppose, who claim that Paul's epistles are strong and firm, but if Paul himself comes to Corinth his weakness will appear. This, of course, is a false statement and mere claims of those who oppose, to disturb the Church and spread false ideas.

entries.section: (2) Paul's authority from God

paragraphs.text: Here Paul declares the truth, which is that he has authority and is strong, both in his epistles and when he visits the Church of Corinth.

entries.section: (2) Paul's authority from God

paragraphs.text: We dare not: we do not allow ourselves to claim authority that is not ours.
Measuring themselves by themselves: that is, they praise themselves and do not compare themselves with the Fathers and the first teachers so as to learn from them.
Paul refuses to commend himself like these who oppose, who deceived themselves by praising themselves and strayed from measuring themselves by the truth, and so went astray.

entries.section: (2) Paul's authority from God

paragraphs.text: Things without our measure: claiming authority or gifts that are not in us.

The measure of the rule which God hath distributed to us: that is, the authority and gifts that God gave us. To reach even unto you: to preach to you and care for you, since as a bishop he is responsible for them before God. Paul affirms that he does not claim any authority or gifts that are not his, as these who oppose do, but uses his authority and gifts to serve and preach to the Corinthians, that they may believe and live with Christ.

entries.section: (2) Paul's authority from God

paragraphs.text: We stretch not ourselves: we do not claim that we preached to you when we did not preach to you, or claim an imaginary authority over you.

Paul affirms that he is the one who preached and founded the Church in Corinth, so he does not claim a false authority over them, but he is the one who came and preached among them as an apostle of Christ, a bishop and head over His Church.

entries.section: (2) Paul's authority from God

paragraphs.text: Things without our measure, that is, other men's labors: that is, what others did of preachers and servants.
Enlarged by you: our ministry and work among you increase.

The Apostle affirms that he does not claim for himself works he did not do and which were done before him, as those who oppose do, who came to Corinth after Paul founded the Church there and left it, and claimed that they were the founders of the Church. Rather, Paul was careful to preach in places where none of the other Apostles had preached. He hopes that the Corinthians will grow in their faith so that they give him the opportunity for his ministry among them to increase, and he may even turn some of them into servants who help him in preaching to the countries around them. All this he will do according to the rule given to him by God, that is, the gifts that the Holy Spirit grants him.

entries.section: (2) Paul's authority from God

paragraphs.text: In the regions beyond you: west of Corinth, that is, Rome and Spain.
Another man's line: the places where other apostles and preachers preached.

Paul continues his wishes, that if the believers in Corinth help him by their steadfastness and spiritual growth, he will not be hindered by their problems, but will care for ministering and preaching in the other regions where no one has preached, and founding churches for Christ.

entries.section: (2) Paul's authority from God

paragraphs.text: Here the Apostle sets down an important spiritual truth, which is not to boast in honor or human achievements, but in God's pleasure and delight in us, and our faith and our enjoyment of His care.

entries.section: (2) Paul's authority from God

paragraphs.text: The Apostle therefore affirms that God's commendation of a person is what approves him, and not that he become proud and commend himself. God's commendation appears in the virtues and spiritual fruits that He gives to His children and in His support of them in their spiritual striving and their service.

Do not be preoccupied with honor and people's praise of you, and do not slip into praising yourself, but care for positive work in knowing God and being joined to Him and, on the other hand, in loving others and helping them, and God's blessings will overflow upon you and you will thank Him, and this will drive you to continual positive work.
Paul's defense of his apostleship and his ministry

entries.section: (1) Paul's defense of his apostleship

paragraphs.text: The Apostle forbade anyone to praise himself like the false teachers who oppose him, and counts this as ignorance and folly, because praise should come from God. But here he is compelled to praise himself in order to establish his apostleship and therefore the teachings he preached to the Corinthians. Because what appears is self-praise, he said to them, bear with me in my folly. He commends them that they were originally distinguished by the virtue of forbearance, and because they love him they will bear with him.

entries.section: (1) Paul's defense of his apostleship

paragraphs.text: I am jealous over you: I love you and refuse that you should stray into evil and false teachings, so that you remain in your sound faith, and my love makes me weary if I see you attached to the world and not to Christ. With godly jealousy: for the glory of God and not for a personal purpose.
I have espoused you: I preached to you and you believed and were joined, as a bride to her heavenly Bridegroom, Christ.

Paul shows his love for the Church of Corinth in that he grieves and is distressed if they turn away from Christ, because by his preaching to them he joined them to Him as a bride, so they must remain in purity like a virgin betrothed to her bridegroom, Christ.

entries.section: (1) Paul's defense of his apostleship

paragraphs.text: Paul continues to show his feelings toward the Church of Corinth, for which he fears lest it be deceived by the ideas of the false teachers, as Satan in the form of the serpent deceived our mother Eve of old. So he asks them to remain in the simplicity of the faith and to beware of the craftiness of the wicked who oppose.

entries.section: (1) Paul's defense of his apostleship

paragraphs.text: Another Jesus: other than Jesus Christ, the Son of the Virgin Mary.
Another spirit: other than the Holy Spirit.

Another gospel: other than the Gospel that Paul preached, which declares that Jesus Christ is God. Paul supposes the existence of teachers who teach another Jesus and another Holy Spirit and another gospel, confirming their teachings with them and with miracles that establish them. All this might be a strong deception that leads the Corinthians away from the faith, so that they would have an acceptable excuse. But the false teachers did not proclaim this; rather they confuse them with strange ideas for the sake of their pride, so why do they follow them? It would have been better for them to hold fast to the sound teaching that Paul preached and reject the ideas of those who oppose.

entries.section: (1) Paul's defense of his apostleship

paragraphs.text: The very chiefest apostles: the foremost Apostles, who are Peter, James and John, whom Christ singled out for certain occasions such as the Transfiguration.

Those who oppose cast doubt on Paul's apostleship, and here he defends it in order also to establish the teachings he taught them, so he declares that he is not only an apostle because Christ appeared to him and entrusted everything to him, but is in no way inferior to the Apostles counted as pillars, because of his labors in the ministry and the gifts God gave him. And his bringing the Gentiles into the faith does not diminish his apostleship, as those who oppose accuse him, but establishes it.

entries.section: (1) Paul's defense of his apostleship

paragraphs.text: Perhaps some of those who oppose accused Paul of weakness in oratory in Greek because he had not studied in the famous Greek schools, although in truth he is distinguished by his eloquence. So Paul defends himself, declaring: even if you judged that I am weak in oratory, that is, common, yet in knowledge and spiritual understanding I am not weak, because I learned everything from Christ directly. This knowledge of mine appeared through my preaching among you and in every place where I preached. Perhaps preaching in the vernacular was a necessity in many cases to explain theological truths to simple people, and this does not diminish the depth of the speaker in any way.

Defend yourself for God's sake and so that you do not cause others to stumble, but let your defense not be for the sake of your honor or to justify your mistakes; rather be humble and apologize for your mistakes, and you will be strong and win the love of those around you.

entries.section: (2) Paul's free ministry

paragraphs.text: I abased myself: I endured providing for my living expenses by the work of my hands.

That ye might be exalted: that you might be joined and grow in the knowledge of God, not occupied with providing for the expenses of me and those with me, so that my free ministry may encourage you to be bound to the love of Christ.

Paul declared the Apostle's right to take his living expenses from those he serves (1 Cor 9:6-12), and those who oppose objected to his apostleship because he does not receive his living expenses from those he serves, so he answered them that he has the right to take these expenses but he gave them up so as not to hinder them from their attachment to Christ and His love.

entries.section: (2) Paul's free ministry

paragraphs.text: I robbed: I accepted gifts from other churches for your ministry, although the believers in Corinth could have provided his expenses, but out of love he did not burden them, so he provided for his needs from the work of his hands and from the donations of other churches.
Other churches: the churches of Macedonia (v. 9), and especially the Church of Philippi.

The Apostle adds, in not burdening the Church of Corinth in providing his expenses, that he supplied his needs from the donations of other churches, and he rose above being a burdensome guest to anyone.

entries.section: (2) Paul's free ministry

paragraphs.text: This boasting: the free ministry in Corinth.
Shall stop me: no one will prevent me from it.
Achaia: the southern region of Greece whose capital is Corinth.

Paul affirms the truth of his words in Christ, who taught him truthfulness, that no member of this Church can stop him from his boasting that he served the Church of Corinth free of charge, or reproach him for it, because it is clear before everyone.

entries.section: (2) Paul's free ministry

paragraphs.text: Paul asks why he did not take his expenses from the Church of Corinth: was it because he did not love them?.. Of course not. And he affirms his words by saying that God knows the measure of his love for them.

entries.section: (2) Paul's free ministry

paragraphs.text: He adds that he will continue to serve the Church of Corinth free of charge so that those who oppose may not find anything against him, that he serves for material gain. For as they tear down Paul's standing, they gain standing and power. The false teachers perhaps perform their teaching free of charge and boast of it, and therefore Paul is careful to serve free of charge so that these who oppose may not use that as a reason to accuse him of wanting material gain.

entries.section: (2) Paul's free ministry

paragraphs.text: Paul exposes the evil of those who oppose him in Corinth, describing them as not true apostles but false, and as crafty, deceiving the simple by their false teachings. Christ did not send them; they only claim it.

entries.section: (2) Paul's free ministry

paragraphs.text: The Apostle goes on to expose those who oppose and to reveal their pretending to be sent by Christ, just as their chief does, Satan, who can appear in the form of an angel of light although he is a devil and his conduct is entirely the opposite of the angels. And because they are servants of Satan, it is no strange thing that they imitate him in deceiving people by pretending to be apostles of Christ, but God will repay them for their evil works with eternal torment if they do not repent.

Offer your love to those around you freely, and do not ask for a material return, and even if they fall short in appreciating your labors or wrong you with words of rebuke and insult, do not give up your love for them. And if you cannot offer them love, at least pray for them.

entries.section: (3) Paul's being compelled to praise himself

paragraphs.text: Paul was compelled to praise himself in order to establish his apostleship, so he says to the Corinthians, do not think that this is folly on my part when I praise myself, for I do not seek any special honor for myself, but I do this for the confirmation of your faith when I establish my apostleship. And even if you think this is folly, bear with me and listen to me as you listened to the false teachers when they praised themselves although they are not apostles of Christ.

entries.section: (3) Paul's being compelled to praise himself

paragraphs.text: That which I speak: that is, what Paul defended his apostleship with, which appeared in the form of boasting.
After the Lord: not like the humble Christ, who did not praise Himself.
As it were foolishly: it appears to be ignorance and folly.
The confidence of boasting: boldness in praising himself.

Paul declares that the opposition of the false teachers is what compelled him to praise himself to establish his apostleship. This is not the way Christ followed and asks His disciples to follow, but it is a special case that compelled him to it. It appears to be folly and needless boldness, but whoever looks closely will know that this is for the confirmation of the faith of the Church of Corinth.

entries.section: (3) Paul's being compelled to praise himself

paragraphs.text: Many: the false teachers.
After the flesh: that is, they are Jews and circumcised and adhere to the Law.

The reason for Paul's boasting is that the false teachers boasted in vain of fleshly things in order to draw people to their false teachings. So Paul was compelled to boast, but for a sound reason, which is to confirm the teachings of Christ that He told him.

entries.section: (3) Paul's being compelled to praise himself

paragraphs.text: Paul commends the Corinthians as being wise and as having borne with the folly of the false teachers in their boasting, so let them complete their forbearance by listening to Paul's defense even if they think it foolish talk. It is wisdom on Paul's part to draw them to listen to him by praising them and by his humility, describing himself as though he were a fool, although in truth the Corinthians were fools in being led after the teachings of those who oppose and giving up the teachings of Paul who preached to them.

entries.section: (3) Paul's being compelled to praise himself

paragraphs.text: Bringeth you into bondage: to the Mosaic ordinances found in the laws of the Law, when they imposed them on them after they became Christians.
Devour you: material exploitation.
Take of you: lords it over you and takes you as prey that he exploits.
Exalt himself: is proud toward you and humbles you.
Smite you on the face: all kinds of insults.
Paul says to the Corinthians, you bore with the false teachers, who enslaved you to the customs of the Law and exploited you and insulted you, so bear with me in my praise of myself.

entries.section: (3) Paul's being compelled to praise himself

paragraphs.text: By way of reproach: the insults that Paul endured.
We have been weak: in humility Paul describes himself and those with him as weak, or those who oppose used to describe them as weak.
Wherein any is bold: the boasting of those who oppose about themselves.

Paul declares that he endured appearing in a guise of weakness and humiliation for the sake of preaching the Gospel of Christ, but now he is compelled to show his strength by praising himself in order to establish his apostleship in the face of false claims and the false teachers' praise of themselves.

Endure insults for God's sake, and defend yourself also for His sake and not to show your honor or out of anger within you and pride. That is, do what you wish, but for one purpose, the glorification of God and not the glorification of yourself.

entries.section: (4) The kinds of labors that Paul endured in his ministry

paragraphs.text: Paul declares that he is no less than the false teachers in his lineage.

Hebrews: named after "Eber," one of the forefathers of "Abraham," or after Abraham, who crossed the Euphrates River to the land of Canaan, so Abraham is called a Hebrew (Gen 14:13) and his descendants Hebrews.
Israelites: named after Israel, who is Jacob, and the meaning of Israel is that he strove with God and prevailed (Gen 32:28), that is, they are God's own people.
The seed of Abraham: who received the promises from God, so they are heirs of these promises, especially since from them comes Christ the Savior.

entries.section: (4) The kinds of labors that Paul endured in his ministry

paragraphs.text: I am more: the false teachers claim to be servants of Christ, but Paul is in truth a servant of God in love and humility, and God sent him to preach, so he is not a forger or a pretender, and therefore he is more. In labours: for the sake of the ministry.
In deaths: his frequent exposure to death.

In this verse Paul shows not only his equality with the false teachers in lineage but also his distinction from them in the ministry, both in the abundance of his labors and his enduring beating and scourging and being thrown into prisons and, more than this, his exposure to death many times.

entries.section: (4) The kinds of labors that Paul endured in his ministry

paragraphs.text: Forty stripes save one: the Law of Moses decreed that the scourging should not exceed forty, so they were accustomed to strike 39 lest they fall into error. And the whip had three thongs, so each stroke was counted as three, that is, he is struck 13 times.
Beaten with rods: most likely by the Romans.

Once was I stoned: that was at Lystra, and he lost consciousness (Acts 14:19). Thrice I suffered shipwreck: this is not mentioned in the Book of Acts, and a fourth time is mentioned that happened after the writing of this epistle when he was going to Rome (Acts 27:41). In the deep: when he was clinging to one of the planks of wood in the sea and spent long hours, whether at night or by day, until God saved him, and this happened in the case of his shipwreck three times. Paul shows some of the labors he endured in his ministry and by which he was distinguished from the false teachers, such as scourging, beating, stoning, shipwreck and his clinging to its planks in the sea.

entries.section: (4) The kinds of labors that Paul endured in his ministry

paragraphs.text: In journeyings: bearing the pain and hardships of travel in his moving between many countries, noting that the means of transport were primitive and so involved much suffering.
Perils of waters: heavy rains that fall on some countries and may cost the lives of many whom they sweep away in their path.
Perils of robbers: highwaymen who attack travelers to seize what they have, so that travelers are exposed to being killed.
Perils by mine own countrymen: that is, the Jews who opposed him, whether in Jerusalem or in the various countries of the world in which he preached.
Perils by the heathen: those among whom he preached in the whole world, and who stirred up many against him to kill him.
Perils in the city: that is, the cities in which he preached and they rose against him and beat him and tried to kill him.
Perils in the wilderness: the deserts he passed through during his missionary journeys.
Perils in the sea: where he traveled by sea in ships many times, and the ships were primitive and were wrecked more than once, and he was exposed to drowning.

Perils among false brethren: the false teachers, who are the Jews who became Christians and opposed his teachings because he showed that the Mosaic customs were a type of Christianity, so there is no need to hold to most of them.

The Apostle showed some of the suffering he met in his ministry that exposed him to death, and this shows his love for God and his worthiness to be called an apostle and servant of the Corinthians more than the false teachers.

entries.section: (4) The kinds of labors that Paul endured in his ministry

paragraphs.text: In watchings: Paul's keeping vigil while preaching and teaching, and also in the work of his hands to provide for his living expenses. In hunger and thirst: he endured at times, during his preaching, extreme poverty, as he did not find his necessary food. In fastings: which he fasted and joined with prayers for his ministry, whether the fasts that the Apostles decreed for the whole Church or additional fasts to seek God's help.
In cold and nakedness: because he was exposed to extreme poverty, so he did not find what would clothe him and warm him while preaching in countries with a cold climate.

The Apostle continues the troubles he bore in his ministry, showing his perseverance in enduring the labors of the ministry and poverty and his need of necessary food and clothing, in addition to fasts, that God might have compassion on him.

entries.section: (4) The kinds of labors that Paul endured in his ministry

paragraphs.text: Paul mentions that what was mentioned above is some of the sufferings, and there are many other labors, lesser than these sufferings, such as his care for the churches in which he preached, as well as the organization of the ministry and following it up.

entries.section: (4) The kinds of labors that Paul endured in his ministry

paragraphs.text: Who is weak: is tired physically or is affected spiritually.
And I am not weak: I pity him and am affected by his weakness, that is, my heart is moved toward him.
Is offended: turns away from the faith.
And I burn not: that is, my heart is filled with zeal and jealousy to rescue him and support him.

Paul makes clear that all the labors mentioned above he went through not only as bodily sufferings, but he was affected psychologically by the sins and falls and deviation from God of many of the believers, so he is zealous to exhort them and show his love for them in order to bring them back to the Church.

entries.section: (4) The kinds of labors that Paul endured in his ministry

paragraphs.text: The false teachers boasted of their knowledge, their eloquence and their lineage, but Paul boasted of his labors and what he endured for the sake of Christ, since it is the proof of his love; and this confirms that he is a true servant.

entries.section: (4) The kinds of labors that Paul endured in his ministry

paragraphs.text: Paul calls God Himself as witness to the truth of his previous words so that they may trust what he says to them.

entries.section: (4) The kinds of labors that Paul endured in his ministry

paragraphs.text: Damascus: an ancient well-known city in Syria.
Governor: the ruler of the city.
Aretas: a title of the kings of the Arabs and of Syria, like Pharaoh for the kings of Egypt.
Kept the city of the Damascenes: watched the gates in order to seize Paul if he tried to escape, because the Jews stirred him up against him.
A window: an opening in a house adjoining the wall.
A basket: a large basket, that is, a large carrying basket.

It seems that this incident was dangerous and Paul's death in it was almost certain, so he mentioned it separately and showed God's protection of him, for he was able to escape from the city while the governor's soldiers were trying to seize him. He went out let down in a basket and went on walking alone in the wilderness until he reached another city.

Look at the love of Christ and what He endured on the cross for your sake, so that you are moved to give yourself for everyone around you and serve with all your strength, confident of God's support and care for you.
Paul's vision, his weakness and his establishing his apostleship

entries.section: (1) Paul's vision of heaven

paragraphs.text: It is not expedient for me to glory: it is not right for a Christian or a servant to boast of himself, for this is a kind of pride; but Paul was compelled to do so in defense of his ministry, so that the Corinthians would not doubt his teaching and the Gospel he preached to them.
Visions: sights seen.
Revelations: a voice from heaven or an angel who explains and makes clear the will of God.

Paul ends his talk about the boasting to which he was compelled, and moves on to another subject, namely the work of God that appears in visions and revelations from heaven to encourage His children; and in this there is no glory for man.

entries.section: (1) Paul's vision of heaven

paragraphs.text: A man: he means himself, but out of humility he did not say that it was he, so that he might teach us to be humble and not to proclaim our personal experiences with pride, but, if we are compelled, to hide ourselves so that God may be glorified. In Christ: a believer in Christ who lives a spiritual life with Him.
In the body: with his body.
Out of the body: with his spirit alone.

The third heaven: the first heaven is the heaven of the birds, the second heaven is the heaven of the stars, and the third heaven is where the angels and the saints dwell, that is, Paradise and the Kingdom. Here Paul declares a vision that he had seen fourteen years before the writing of this Epistle, that is, in the year AD 43. Because of the greatness and power of the vision, he declares his inability to determine whether he saw it in his spirit alone, or whether God lifted him up to heaven in his spirit and body to see the glories of Paradise.

entries.section: (1) Paul's vision of heaven

paragraphs.text: Paradise: a word of Persian origin meaning a garden. Paradise is the place where the righteous wait until the day of judgment, when He will transfer them to the Kingdom. It is called the Paradise of bliss or of joy because the state of the spirits there is one of joy and bliss.
Not lawful: no man is able to express them, because they are beyond words and imagination.
Paul declares that he saw great things in Paradise which cannot be expressed, because they are higher than all human conceptions.

entries.section: (1) Paul's vision of heaven

paragraphs.text: Paul affirms that boasting is to be in the grace of God, as it appeared in this vision, and not in man's works and achievements. So he does not boast of anything, and if he is compelled, he will boast of his shortcomings and weaknesses, which Christ completes; that is, he boasts only in the grace of God, while keeping his humility.

entries.section: (1) Paul's vision of heaven

paragraphs.text: Paul shows that if he speaks of things he has accomplished, this is not foolishness, because he is truthful in every word and was compelled to do so in order to confirm his teaching and preaching. But he returns and affirms that he avoids boasting needlessly, lest he show himself great and be proud in the eyes of others; he does not desire that, but only to confirm and establish his teaching. That is, he is able at any time to show his abilities and distinction, but he will not do this, so as not to fall into pride; for his way, and the way of all Christians, is humility and the hiding of virtues.
Do not show your superiority over others, but praise them and encourage them; and if they praise you, direct your thanks to God, so that pride does not war against you.

entries.section: (2) Paul's boasting in his weakness

paragraphs.text: Exalted: be proud.
The revelations: the visions and the gifts.
A thorn in the flesh: an illness.
The messenger of Satan: Satan wanted to hinder Paul from the ministry and to harm him, and God permitted it for his benefit, so that he might keep his humility.
To buffet me: to mistreat me.

Paul declared the grace of God toward him through an illness that God permitted, namely a weakness in the eyes (Gal 4:15), which forced him to dictate his epistles to others, and if he wrote anything himself he wrote it in large letters (Gal 6:11); and also sores and pus that afflicted his body, on which he used to place pieces of cloth, and these soiled pieces of cloth used to heal the sick (Acts 19:12). It is to be noted that the illness was lasting, because it was a constant protection for him from pride.

entries.section: (2) Paul's boasting in his weakness

paragraphs.text: Paul declares that he prayed three times that God would heal him of his illness; and because his prayer was made in reliance and surrender to God, He declared to him that he should not ask again, because this illness was by His permission for his benefit, and that the grace of God would support him and suffice for all his needs, so that he would not be hindered in anything in his life or ministry. Rather, He declared to him something more than this: that his bodily weakness would not make him weak in anything, but his strength would be made perfect by the grace of God, so that he became joyful and proud of this illness because it was a constant cause for the power of God to work in him. Thus Paul experienced God every day through His making up for what he lacked and helping him to live, and he became not like the rest but better than they, because he was made perfect by the power of God.

entries.section: (2) Paul's boasting in his weakness

paragraphs.text: Here Paul repeats his joy in his weakness and in everything that befalls him of persecutions, whether insults and abuse, or poverty, or any suffering for the sake of Christ, because through them he experiences the work of God in him. For when he feels his weakness and humbles himself before God, he immediately becomes strong through His support of him.

Do not be distressed by your weakness or your troubles, because they are your way to enjoy the work of God in you. Accept them with thanksgiving, and be humble and lowly before Him, and the divine blessings will pour down upon you and you will become distinguished from those around you.

entries.section: (3) Paul's proof of his apostleship

paragraphs.text: Paul affirms that boasting of personal achievements is folly, but the Corinthians compelled him to do this, because they did not defend him before the false teachers who boasted of themselves and cast doubt on his apostleship and teaching, but kept silent; and this was weakness and sin on their part, especially since Paul's ministry is no less than the ministry and preaching of the outstanding Apostles, namely Peter, James and John. But Paul feels within himself that he is nothing, and he says all this for the benefit of his hearers, so that they may stand firm in the teachings of Christ which he preached to them.

entries.section: (3) Paul's proof of his apostleship

paragraphs.text: Here Paul proves his apostleship by the miracles he performed in the Church of Corinth, while he was suffering tribulations and persecutions from them; therefore they ought to have believed in his apostleship and teaching, and not been disturbed and believed the doubts raised by the opponents.

entries.section: (3) Paul's proof of his apostleship

paragraphs.text: Paul asks the Corinthians in reproach what was lacking in his preaching to them and his care, for their church received complete care like the rest of the churches that the other Apostles founded. Then he shames them by saying that he did lack one thing for them, namely not burdening them with paying for his living expenses, and he did this so that they would not say that he asked a reward for his ministry among them. And he corrects himself and asks them to forgive him for wronging them in this, since he deprived them of this grace, which is giving to the one who serves them; but he was compelled to do so lest they doubt his ministry, which he gave them free of charge.

entries.section: (3) Paul's proof of his apostleship

paragraphs.text: It is understood from this verse that before writing this Epistle Paul had visited Corinth twice, and he declares his readiness to visit them a third time and to serve them without material payment, and there are two reasons for this:
1- That he loves them and seeks their salvation, not their money and their gifts.
2- That he is a father, and it is the custom that fathers spend on their children for all their needs, and not the reverse, although when the fathers are in need the children must care for them.

entries.section: (3) Paul's proof of his apostleship

paragraphs.text: I will gladly spend: I will give and offer what I have of money for your needs.
And be spent: I will give my life for your service.

Paul declares his joy in giving whatever money he possesses in the ministry, indeed in offering his life and giving it even to death for the preaching to and service of his children in Corinth. But it is very sad that the more love he showed them, the less love they showed him in return, that is, they doubt him and do not defend him before the opponents; and this is very hard on the heart of anyone who loves and sacrifices. By this he reproaches them gently, so that they may respond to his love and defend his preaching to them, and so stand firm in the faith.

entries.section: (3) Paul's proof of his apostleship

paragraphs.text: But be it so: Paul accepts their weak love and continues to love them more and more.

Paul sent Titus and those with him to collect contributions for the poor of Jerusalem, and the opponents accused him of collecting these contributions in order to take from them for himself, and that he pretends to spend on his needs from the work of his hands and took nothing for himself from the church of Corinth, whereas in fact he does take, by means of what Titus collects; and this is a false accusation. But Paul says: if you accuse me of being crafty, then I am crafty for the sake of your salvation, and I caught you with guile when I offered a love that gave itself without return, to win your souls for Christ. This is the craftiness that he practiced, and not craftiness for the sake of material gain.

entries.section: (3) Paul's proof of his apostleship

paragraphs.text: Paul affirms that he received nothing material from them, whether by himself or by means of his helpers such as Titus and those with him whom he sent to collect contributions for the needy believers in Jerusalem. Titus took nothing for himself, and none of his companions either, but they walked in the same manner as Paul in the ministry, that is, ministry free of charge.

entries.section: (3) Paul's proof of his apostleship

paragraphs.text: Paul denies that by his previous words he wishes to display his righteousness and enjoy the praise of the Church of Corinth, because he feels that he is speaking before God, united with Christ who is in him, and intends only to establish them in the faith and in all the teachings he preached to them, so that this leads to the growth of their spiritual edification.

entries.section: (3) Paul's proof of his apostleship

paragraphs.text: I shall not find you such as I wish: I find you walking in evil and not firm in the faith. And that I shall be found by you such as you do not wish: my rebuke and punishment will appear against those who persist in evil and in causing those around them to stumble.

Paul declares his fear that some of the believers in Corinth continue in evil, such as creating quarrels and factions, judging one another, and stirring up doubts and confusions that make many stumble, and a pride that leads to envy and anger, so that they depart from life with Christ.

entries.section: (3) Paul's proof of his apostleship

paragraphs.text: Paul continues his fears that he may find many in the Church of Corinth still walking in evil, such as fornication connected with pride, and the quarrels mentioned in the previous verse; and this will grieve Paul very much and make him humbled before Satan, who made his children fall into these sins. But he will accept this from God, and will be moved and weep over them, and will try to admonish them and bring them back by repentance to God. He mentions this in the hope that it may stir the feelings of the believers who are firm in the faith, so that they may try to call these wicked ones to repentance before Paul comes.

Offer your love to others without waiting for their response to you, because God loves you, so you respond to Him with love for His children; and know that your love will bear its fruit in their hearts, even if after a while. But you will win the experience of God's mercies and the beholding of His love and the knowledge of Him.
Paul's warning and his call to the stubborn to repent

entries.section: (1) A warning to the unrepentant

paragraphs.text: Paul visited Corinth in AD 53 (Acts 18:1-18), then visited it a second time in AD 56 (1 Cor 16:5-8), and he is about to visit them a third time, as he mentions here. He affirms his following words as a decision by which he judges the stubborn, and supports it with the testimony of two with him, as the Law of Moses requires, and these are Sosthenes (1 Cor 1:1) and Timothy (2 Cor 1:1), both of them disciples of Paul.

entries.section: (1) A warning to the unrepentant

paragraphs.text: I have told you before: Paul declared that he would discipline the stubborn if they did not repent (ch. 10:
2, ch. 12:21.) I say beforehand: before I come to you in Corinth I affirm that I shall punish the unrepentant.
The second time: the second visit to Corinth, which took place in AD 56.
All the rest: those who sinned and whose sins have not appeared or been exposed, or those who did not sin but are exposed to falling into fornication and stumbling sins.

Paul affirms with firmness and with his apostolic authority that he will punish those who persist in wrongdoing and refuse repentance when he visits them the third time. This shows the need for Church penalties when there is persistence in sin, such as depriving the offenders of fellowship in the Church, that is, of partaking of the Holy Mysteries.

entries.section: (1) A warning to the unrepentant

paragraphs.text: A proof of Christ speaking: Paul's apostolic authority, which Christ gave him.

Here Paul affirms his apostolic authority which he received from Christ, because Christ is God and His authority is of utmost power; He is not weak before the stubborn, but strong and able to protect the Church, to establish the believers and to cut off the wicked until they repent.

entries.section: (1) A warning to the unrepentant

paragraphs.text: Crucified through weakness: the crucified Christ appeared as a weak man, indeed in utmost humiliation and shame.
Lives by the power of God: He rose by His divinity, and He lives forever.

Weak in Him: the servants of Christ appear weak in what they endure for His sake during their ministry. We shall live with Him: we enjoy His fellowship and His work in us during our life on earth, so we are not disturbed by the insults and wrongs of others.

Toward you: we speak with authority, punish the offenders and hold fast to the firm teachings of Christ. The Apostle here again affirms his authority and strength in Christ; just as Christ appeared weak in His crucifixion, but in truth He is God, able to do all things, so we also appear weak in the insults and opposition we endure, but by the power of Christ we are able to lead the Church in the way of the Kingdom and to cut off the opponents.

Your strength has its source in Christ. So proclaim the truth with courage, whatever pressures you face. And if you endure insults, be sure that the truth that is in you is stronger than the evil that is in others. Do not doubt yourself, and pray for them, and surround your proclamation of the truth with love, so that people feel that you seek their good, and in the end submit to you for God's sake.

entries.section: (2) Examination of the faith for the sake of repentance

paragraphs.text: Some believers of the Church of Corinth opposed Paul and tested him, doubting his apostleship, and here he calls them to examine themselves, whether they have the sound, living faith, or whether, because of their sins, they are rejected by Christ. What is required now is not to examine their teacher but to examine themselves, so that they may repent of their sins and walk in the upright faith. And the examination of the faith is not only making sure of religious beliefs, but also shows itself in spiritual fruits and is done under the guidance of the Fathers and spiritual guides.

entries.section: (2) Examination of the faith for the sake of repentance

paragraphs.text: Paul assures them that if they examine themselves in truth, they will discover that they are rejected by Christ because of their persistence in sin and their refusal to submit to the Church and its teachings, and they will then be certain that Paul and his helpers among the servants have the sound faith and are not rejected by Christ.

entries.section: (2) Examination of the faith for the sake of repentance

paragraphs.text: Paul shows the feelings of his tender fatherhood in his prayer for the Corinthians, that they may turn away from evil and do good, and so be righteous before God, not so that Paul may praise that his children are righteous, he who served them and preached to them so that they became so, but so that they may enjoy doing good and God's pleasure in them. Rather, his self-giving and love for them show that he is ready to appear as though rejected and in the wrong, so long as they are righteous; and he is not in truth rejected, but only seems to be rejected, as when it is said of him that he was more severe than he should have been and threatened them with punishment although they were righteous. He accepts being accused in this way, but what he desires is that they do good works that make them pleasing before God.

entries.section: (2) Examination of the faith for the sake of repentance

paragraphs.text: Paul affirms his adherence to the truth, who is God, in all his conduct and ministry; so he judges the offenders only by the truth, and if they repent he rejoices in them, and they become righteous before God.

entries.section: (2) Examination of the faith for the sake of repentance

paragraphs.text: We are weak: we do not mind appearing, for your sake, in the form of weakness.
You are strong: you walk well, keeping away from the former sins and rejecting them.
Your perfection: your striving toward Christian perfection.

Paul affirms his fatherhood in accepting the judgment of weakness and error against him, so that he may judge that his Corinthian children are strong and righteous; indeed he desires that they grow in their spiritual life until they become perfect.

entries.section: (2) Examination of the faith for the sake of repentance

paragraphs.text: Being absent: at the time of sending this Epistle, when he was staying in Macedonia.
Sharply: determining a penalty for the offenders and cutting them off from the Church.
Being present: in the midst of the Church of Corinth.

For edification and not for destruction: to help souls to live with God, and not as revenge or to destroy anyone. Paul declares that he uses his apostolic authority for edification, and that the purpose of warning sinners so that they repent is to be rid of carrying out any penalty on the offenders. His fatherhood desires that no one be punished and seeks the salvation of all.

Have a fatherhood toward all people, so that you forget yourself however much people wrong you, and seek their salvation, even if they are justified and their goodness appears before others, and at the same time you are accused of wrongdoing, even unjustly. What matters is that you draw all souls to God.

entries.section: (3) Closing wishes and greeting of peace

paragraphs.text: Rejoice: in the fellowship of Christ and the Kingdom that awaits you.
Be perfect: strive toward perfection.
Be of good comfort: by the work of the Holy Spirit in you and in the Church.
Be of one mind: care for unity of thought and opinion and keep away from factions and divisions.
Live in peace: be at peace with one another, even if that requires giving up some of your rights and bearing with one another.
At the close of the Epistle Paul shows his wishes for the believers in Corinth: joy, comfort, the enjoyment of peace, and the blessings of God which overflow upon those who walk in love and peace.

entries.section: (3) Closing wishes and greeting of peace

paragraphs.text: Since the first centuries Christians have been accustomed to greet and kiss one another as a sign of love and purity of heart, and the Church in the Divine Liturgy still calls her children to do this, so they greet one another by the touching of hands, men with men and women with women.

entries.section: (3) Closing wishes and greeting of peace

paragraphs.text: The saints: the believers who are sanctified in Christ and set apart for Him.
After Paul called them to peace with one another, he sends them the greeting of peace from the believers in the churches of Macedonia, where he is writing the Epistle.

entries.section: (3) Closing wishes and greeting of peace

paragraphs.text: Paul closes his Epistle with the blessing of the Holy Trinity: the Son, the Father and the Holy Spirit. He put the Son before the Father because through His redemption we obtained reconciliation with God, and then through the Holy Spirit we receive all the blessings of redemption in the Church. From this the Church has been accustomed to close her prayers with this blessing.
May you gladden the hearts of others with beautiful wishes, to encourage them and urge them to every good work.
